chunks.text: Durov explains how Telegram serves over a billion users with about 40 core engineers, hires through coding contests, obsesses over speed and detail, and became profitable via premium subscriptions and context-based ads instead of selling user data. Much of the talk covers freedom, privacy and discipline.

chunks.heading: Telegram's lean team: 40 engineers, automation, and self-built infrastructure
chunks.text:
- Telegram's core engineering team is about 40 people (backend, frontend, designers, sysadmins). Pavel argues headcount doesn't translate to product quality: with too many people, "90% of their time will be spent on coordinating the small pieces of work they're responsible for."
- Idle employees demotivate everyone else, and they start inventing problems inside the team.
- Refusing to let people hire helpers forces automation. Telegram runs nearly 100,000 servers across several continents. Managing them by hand would take thousands or tens of thousands of staff, so algorithms run the fleet. He says this is more scalable, more reliable and more resilient to geopolitical change.
- He treats humans as attack vectors, so a self-running distributed system raises both security and speed.
- Telegram's stack is built in-house from scratch: servers, database engines, web servers and the programming language for the client API. He says this shrinks the attack surface. The one exception is Linux on the back end.
- He claims Telegram is the only popular messenger with open-source reproducible builds on both Android and iOS. Apps have been open source on GitHub since 2013.

chunks.heading: Hiring: coding contests, selective and slow
chunks.text:
- Pavel hires through competitions: "What can be better than a competition?" Coding contests let anyone prove skill. If the data is thin, he repeats the contest with a new task.
- A candidate who competed in 10 contests since age 14-16 and won 8 is a strong signal of consistency.
- Contest tasks are real product work, such as a tricky profile-page animation for the open-source Android app. Telegram gets both a hire and the best solution.
- He prefers people who have never worked at a big company, because big companies "shift responsibility" and nobody knows who owns what.
- He prefers hiring users of the product over ex-Google profiles from LinkedIn.
- He promotes contests on his large social platforms, so finding engineers and designers is never a problem.
- He cares about A players versus B players. Firing one weak Android engineer made a third hire unnecessary and raised output. B players demote A players because everyone can see who isn't competent.
- Hiring bar: he hires only when "ultimately certain it's the best option." A careless developer can add inefficiencies worth tens of millions of dollars.
- He says the key trait is the ability to focus on one task for a long time.

chunks.heading: Speed, simplicity and craft as product principles
chunks.text:
- Speed is a core priority. In 2009 Mark Zuckerberg's team asked why VK loaded faster than Facebook. Pavel says even a 50 ms difference is felt subconsciously, and faster code means fewer servers and lower cost.
- Scale argument: half a second of delay, times dozens of opens a day, times a billion users, is "centuries, millennia lost for humanity."
- He asks every developer to keep asking whether something can be done more simply and efficiently.
- He says getting rid of features is essential to scale. Existing users will ask for more complexity, so relying only on their feedback is a trap.
- Design details he describes obsessing over:
  - A four-color shifting default chat background. He reviewed several thousand variations, with pattern overlays that must not distract and must be vector-based.
  - Message send and delete animations. Deleted messages dissolve in a "Thanos snap" effect while neighbors close the gap at the same time.
  - Vector stickers of only a few KB to 20-30 KB, with 180 frames at 60 fps on all devices, launched 3 years 8 months before WhatsApp's stickers. He says WhatsApp used GIF/WebM instead.
  - Custom animated emoji: up to 100 per message without crashing the device.
- He wants animations to create a feeling without causing distraction. His test is whether users feel even a tiny bit of joy.
- The hard part is making it beautiful and fast on the oldest, cheapest phones.
- He says going back to another messenger after a few weeks of Telegram "feels like a serious downgrade."

chunks.heading: Shipping pace and being first
chunks.text:
- Telegram pushes several meaningful features every month, and Pavel claims it out-innovates the industry.
- Examples he says Telegram shipped first, with competitors copying later (sometimes down to identical timestamps):
  - The auto-delete timer in 2013 secret chats. WhatsApp copied it about 7 years later.
  - Message replies with a quoted snippet and vertical line.
  - Message editing.
  - End-to-end encryption in secret chats, in 2013. WhatsApp rolled out around 2016.
- On deadlines, he accepts only ambitious ones. His benchmark: "I built the first version of VK in just two weeks. Why would you need three weeks?"
- He uses Telegram itself for all team collaboration, which exposes product gaps early.

chunks.heading: Encryption design: the trade-off behind opt-in secret chats
chunks.text:
- Telegram has never shared a single private message with any government or agency. Cloud data is encrypted and the keys are split across jurisdictions. No employee can access private messages, and the design means a single point of failure can't be created.
- Pavel says he would rather shut Telegram down in a country than add a back door. The EU push to weaken encryption would just mean Telegram leaves that market.
- Secret chats are end-to-end encrypted but limited by design: no screenshots, no forwarding, no large groups, no multi-device sync.
- Reasons he gives for keeping end-to-end encryption opt-in:
  - Large communities of up to 200,000 members with persistent history.
  - Channels, high-volume bots, and multi-device support.
  - Not losing shared documents.
- Result: a hybrid where users choose the level of protection. He calls secret chats "the most secure means of communication today" for the paranoid.

chunks.heading: Monetization without selling user data
chunks.text:
- Telegram was first profitable in 2024. Pavel says it has lost money for him personally and he has never sold a share.
- Premium subscription (launched 2022) is priced around $4-5 a month with 50+ extra features. It has over 15 million paid subscribers and more than $500M in revenue this year, and is growing fast.
- His principle is to keep all existing features free and add extras for business and power users.
- Ads are context-based (by channel topic), not targeted. He says Telegram leaves about 80% of potential value on the table by refusing to use personal data. There is also no newsfeed.
- Mini apps: Telegram takes a 5% commission on in-app purchases through Apple/Google payments. Developers earn from games and tools. He cites developers making $3M, $10M and $12M in months.
- Channel owners get a 50/50 split of ad revenue, paid out via TON.
- Gifts: blockchain-based collectibles shown on profiles, built on TON. The Snoop Dogg collection sold $12M in 30 minutes. Early items sold around $5 and later traded from $10,000.
- TON came from the 2018-19 project. His brother designed a sharded blockchain for scale, the SEC dispute ended the project, and the open-source community took it over. Now all payments, usernames and withdrawals on Telegram run on TON.
- He owns 100% of Telegram with no shareholders, which lets him hold to principles.
- Personal finance: he bought his first few thousand bitcoin in 2013 at about $700 each, held through the drop to about $300, and says Bitcoin funds his lifestyle. He expects it to reach $1M.

chunks.heading: Building VK: from a student site to a social network
chunks.text:
- He started coding at 10 and built games at 11. Scarcity of games and entertainment pushed him to build, and he thinks scarcity drives creativity.
- At university he built a site with digital exam answers and lectures, then forums, friends lists, photo albums and blogs. It grew to tens of thousands of users across universities.
- A classmate asked if he was building a Russian Facebook. Seeing Facebook showed him which features to cut in order to scale.
- He built VK alone for nearly a year: backend, frontend, design, support and marketing (announcements and competitions).
- His brother's first-step advice was to build just the login module and prepopulate the database, so you can see the first working behavior.
- Stack: PHP, MySQL, Debian, memcached, then nginx. He scaled with extra servers, database splits and sharding.
- Around 2008 his brother and a friend rewrote the search, ad engine and messaging data engines in C/C++. That made VK among the fastest-loading sites.
- Growth brought DDoS attacks, which intensified on days of share-sale negotiations.
- He argues that alone for a year taught him every part of a social platform and how much one person can do. He now sets deadlines on that basis.

chunks.heading: Competition, focus and a niche as a route to success
chunks.text:
- He credits competition for progress: in schools and in hiring, removing competition removes winners too, and kids then compete in video games instead.
- He cites education systems built on ruthless competition (China, South Korea, Singapore, Japan) outpacing those that removed it.
- Strategy on differentiation: don't copy the majority. Set your own agenda and pursue mastery in a niche over time until you are the world's top expert, since few people stay consistent.
- Information diet: curate sources instead of living on algorithmic feeds. Ask "who benefits from me reading this?" about news.
- Habits he links to productivity: no phone beyond occasional Telegram testing, long sleep, quiet thinking in the morning, and avoiding being "told what to think about" first thing.
- His view on being reachable: "the more connected and accessible you are, the less productive you are."
- Self-discipline: 300 push-ups and 300 squats every morning, gym 5-6 times a week, no alcohol, tobacco, coffee, pills or drugs for 20+ years. He says action creates energy: "do first and then feel."
- Leadership on Elon Musk: he says a founder must be ready to be unpleasant, insult inferior work and fire without remorse, since an entrepreneur "sacrifices peace of mind."

chunks.heading: Refusing government pressure in practice
chunks.text:
- 2011: he publicly refused a Russian prosecutor's demand to take down opposition groups on VK. He expected prison, and the episode led to leaving VK and launching Telegram.
- 2018: Russia demanded encryption keys and banned Telegram. Telegram rotated millions of IP addresses automatically, and volunteers worldwide ran proxies ("digital resistance"). Telegram spent millions of dollars on it, and Russian infrastructure was disrupted by the blocking.
- Apple blocked Telegram updates for over four weeks. Pavel went public via his channel and was ready to withdraw from the Russian market. Apple approved the update minutes before his deadline.
- Iran: Telegram let proxy operators monetize with a pinned ad chat. He says about 50 million people there still use it despite the ban.
- 2024-25: after his French arrest, he says French intelligence asked him to restrict conservative channels around the Romanian election and Moldovan channels. He refused, disclosed it publicly, and never signs NDAs with such parties.
- Moderation: Telegram has published daily takedown reports for years, with hundreds of CSAM and terrorism channels removed daily and millions of pieces of content weekly. It protects peaceful speech on all sides as long as it does not call for violence.
- Principle: "I would rather lose everything I have than yield to this pressure."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov recounts his August 2024 arrest in France and explains how Telegram runs: profitable without harvesting user data, compliant through legal process, and committed to privacy over government back doors. It teaches monetization aligned with values, product-led influence, and refusing to compromise user trust.

chunks.heading: Pavel's arrest in France and how he describes it
chunks.text:
- He flew into Paris in August 2024 as a tourist (heading on to Finland, no business meetings) and was met at the airport by police, who read him a list of about 16 charges.
- He was held 4 days in a roughly 7 m² windowless cell with a thin mattress, no pillow and a blinking light, with no phone or contact beyond his assistant.
- He says the charges were about crimes other users committed on Telegram, not anything he did. No one claims he personally took part in drug sales, organized crime or similar.
- He was confused about why police skipped the normal route. As a French citizen his home address is in his passport, and the French consulate is two floors below Telegram's Dubai office. He had met French officials there before and was "happy to just go two floors below".
- He found the public announcements and press coverage unusual. A policeman told him newspapers were writing "everything but truth".
- Hardest part: being cut off from his ill, elderly mother and his children.

chunks.heading: The "failure to cooperate" claim
chunks.text:
- French authorities alleged Telegram ignored judicial requests. Pavel says it never received a single legally binding request from France.
- Under the EU Digital Services Act there is a defined process for such requests, and Telegram's privacy policy documents it. Telegram had run a Belgian company handling these requests for about a year before his arrest.
- Telegram discloses IP address and phone number of criminal suspects when it receives a court order signed by a judge. This concerns identification data only, not private messages, which he says Telegram could not disclose even if it wanted to.
- After his arrest, French requests started arriving through the proper channel and Telegram answered them. He says French officials then publicly celebrated Telegram "now cooperating" as if it were new, which he thinks gave a false picture, "bad for Telegram" and worse for France's image.
- He says prosecutors could have found the process by Googling it in "about 6 minutes".

chunks.heading: Complicity theory and Telegram's compliance posture
chunks.text:
- Pavel says his lawyers call the complicity theory unprecedented in France. Past cases targeted small niche apps built for criminals, with no bank accounts or audits.
- He argues Telegram is the opposite of that profile:
  - Audited by a Big Four firm.
  - Works with major financial institutions.
  - Issued bonds with JP Morgan's help.
  - Spends millions per quarter on legal compliance and content moderation.
  - Operates in almost 200 countries.
- His logic: a platform used by a billion people (every eighth person on the planet) will always have some bad actors. Blaming the founder for that would be like jailing a president for every armed robbery in his country.
- Current status: not on trial. He is under a judicial investigation to decide whether there is enough evidence for one.
- He is under "judicial control", which limits his travel. He has been allowed to go to Dubai and back, and only has to answer questions in France every 4 to 5 months. After almost 8 months he says he still does not know the exact claim against him.
- Costs: he cannot sign documents for his kids in Dubai, cannot see his mother, and runs the company remotely, less efficiently. France is under 1% of Telegram users (he says about half of 1%).

chunks.heading: Telegram's business model and product record
chunks.text:
- Telegram became profitable in 2024, with more than half a billion dollars in profit.
- It reached 1 billion monthly users and is the second most popular messaging app in the world.
- Monetization avoids harvesting personal data for targeted ads. Paid subscriptions are voluntary and the core service is free.
- He claims dozens of features now standard in messaging apps (about 100 by his list) first appeared on Telegram. Examples he gives: replying to messages, sharing links and documents, text formatting. Rivals copied them 3 to 8 years later.
- Telegram doesn't promote channels. A new user sees an empty chat list, and every channel must be deliberately searched for and joined. He calls this neutral: people judge for themselves.

chunks.heading: Privacy, encryption and back doors
chunks.text:
- He rejects back doors on technical grounds: no exclusive back door exists, so any back door can be exploited by foreign agents and hackers, endangering all users.
- Criminals would switch to niche apps or VPNs, so only law-abiding citizens would be hurt.
- He cites a French Senate law passed the month before that effectively banned encryption. The National Assembly shot it down, but a French public he says was unaware of it. The European Commission's early-April proposal pushes similar back doors at EU level. He says no country has banned encryption so far.
- He chose not to base his team in the US partly because of gag orders, which he says let the government force an engineer to implement a back door and not even tell the employer. He took US legal advice and decided it was a poor place for a privacy-oriented platform.
- His stance: if a country forced Telegram to disclose private messaging data, "we would discontinue providing services in that country". He says this is why he left Russia.
- No one has demanded "the keys" from him in France, and technically such keys don't exist. If asked, "you'll be among the first to learn about it".
- Biggest privacy risk in his view: state actors compromising the device itself via zero-day vulnerabilities, and spyware like Pegasus (he says he was among those who had it installed on their phones around 8 years earlier, per leaked reports). Checking for known compromises is possible but nothing is certain.
- On quantum computing: encryption has to evolve and quantum-secure methods exist, but he won't claim confidence, since state actors may have capabilities nobody discloses.
- Personal practice: he doesn't carry or regularly use a phone (about a year, no SIM). He sees it as distracting and a privacy risk. He tests Telegram on a device twice a week for product updates, and otherwise works from laptop or iPad to avoid consuming short-form content.

chunks.heading: Governments, free speech and the EU
chunks.text:
- On governments' motives, he's measured: officials are "trying to solve the problems that they see using the tools that they have", not necessarily running a conspiracy, even if the result harms freedoms. Interior ministers say encryption is the problem, without seeing two or three steps ahead.
- Recurring justifications for weakening privacy are protecting children and fighting crime.
- He argues freedoms erode gradually when populations take them for granted. People who grew up in the Soviet Union, like him, remember having only three TV channels (all about the Communist Party) and two kinds of ice cream, and so value free markets and free speech.
- He says the DSA requires removing content that one EU member state demands be removed across the whole EU, with appeals taking years and fines or bans for slow compliance.
- He recounts a Latvian border officer telling him the EU felt like the Soviet Union again.
- He still describes France as a country that respects human rights and says he plans to return after the case.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A political keynote, not a growth talk. Durov draws on 20 years of running VK and Telegram to argue that governments use child-protection pretexts, mass surveillance and selective enforcement to control platforms. The product and leadership lessons are indirect: refuse political deals, don't hold user data you can't protect, and expect bans to fail.

chunks.heading: The ship of personal freedoms is already sinking
chunks.text:
- Pavel opens with the Titanic: passengers stayed aboard for almost 2 hours after the iceberg strike, lifeboats left half empty, and panic came only in the last half hour, when it was too late.
- He says the ship of personal freedoms has already hit the iceberg, and that freedoms have eroded almost everywhere in the world.
- His authority comes from running large social media platforms for exactly 20 years. He says he has seen the PR tricks, legal tricks, political tricks, manipulations and official excuses governments use to take away basic rights.
- His main worry is that tactics used by authoritarian regimes in Russia, China and Iran are now being used in some Western countries.
- He says "there is no second West" and "no backup civilization". If Western freedom sinks, he expects the rest of the world to follow. Dissidents used to flee to the West, and in a decade or two they may not be able to tell whether they have left a repressive homeland or entered another open-air prison.

chunks.heading: Why age verification and teen social media bans fail
chunks.text:
- Pavel cites the European Commission's push to require ID before anyone can access social media. The stated reason is child protection, via a ban for under-16s that needs age verification.
- He says the experiment has already been run in Russia. Russia banned Telegram, then the largest social platform there, because Telegram refused demands for mass surveillance and censorship.
- Even so, 95% of Russian teenagers still use Telegram every month, through VPNs.
- Russia has invested billions in fighting VPNs. It bans hundreds of VPNs every month using IP addresses and traffic patterns, and installed surveillance hardware in every data center of every internet provider. He says it failed anyway.
- Iran has blocked Telegram since 2018, and the majority of the population still uses it.
- His conclusion is that banning social media for part of the population just pushes people onto VPNs. Forcing teenagers onto VPNs unlocks nasty, illegal, fringe content and previously banned websites, so children end up in more danger than before.
- He points to the UK Online Safety Act. Publicly it was sold as protecting children, but in a submission to the High Court of England published the year before, the British government said the main part of the Act "was aimed at capturing large platforms with significant influence over public discourse". Pavel reads this as child protection used as a pretext for control over political speech.

chunks.heading: "Protect the children" as a pretext that bypasses debate
chunks.text:
- He argues that "child protection" triggers ancient, deep parts of the brain. Everyone fears for their offspring, so it "bypasses logic. It bypasses debate. It bypasses rationality."
- He says authoritarian regimes over the last century have smuggled all kinds of repressive legislation in under this guise.
- The same justification is used for "chat control", the European Commission's 5-year effort to force every messaging app to put a backdoor in its encryption. Every private message and photo sent on apps like Telegram or WhatsApp would be automatically monitored, with alerts to authorities if the system detects something illegal.
- The French government has tried a national version. The French Senate approved a mass surveillance law, which got stuck in the National Assembly. France's justification was fighting crime, terrorism and drug trafficking.
- He calls the trade of essential liberty for temporary safety "always a scam" and quotes Benjamin Franklin: "Those who are willing to give up their essential liberty for some temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety."

chunks.heading: Why surveillance does not stop crime but does harm ordinary people
chunks.text:
- Pavel asks whether people in Russia or Iran feel safer than 10-15 years ago. They lost many freedoms and he doubts they gained safety.
- Once police can read messages, criminals switch first to more secure tools: VPNs, private secret apps, even their own encrypted messenger, which he says AI now lets them code themselves. "The criminals will be fine." Law-abiding citizens bear the cost.
- Personal experience at VK: about 15 years earlier, while he ran VK, the largest Russian social network, police data requests began to look odd. VK then disclosed private message contents in some cases with an official justification, unlike Telegram today, which he says never does.
- The people named in these requests had nothing to do with the crimes described. VK investigated the investigators and found the police were corrupt: they sought innocent people's private messages to blackmail them, sell their data to criminals and harass them.
- He says this can happen in the West too. Last year a French tax official was caught selling financial data on holders of large crypto assets and other wealth to criminals.
- He links such leaks to a catastrophic rise in kidnappings in France: over 40 victims in the first 3 months of 2026, with people tortured, harmed and humiliated. His point is that the government collected too much data and failed to protect it, yet now wants more (private messages, and IDs of everyone on social media).

chunks.heading: Selective enforcement of laws as a tool of control
chunks.text:
- Pavel describes a method used by authoritarians for decades and now exported from East to West, in steps:
  - Introduce a large number of laws.
  - Overburden an industry with excessive, mutually exclusive, contradictory regulation, so compliance is impossible and every entrepreneur or CEO can be treated as a criminal.
  - Choose carefully whom to persecute. A loyal owner who complies with unlawful political demands is ignored by law enforcement and courts. An owner who stands up for citizens' constitutional rights or refuses political demands gets full enforcement.
  - When criticized, the response is always "we're just enforcing the law".
- He says he experienced this in Russia, with a criminal investigation against him in 2013.
- Elon Musk's claim: he said the European Commission offered him a secret deal to censor certain political narratives on his platform in exchange for not enforcing certain fines and laws. Musk said he refused, while most other platforms accepted. His company was then hit with a 120 million euro fine for seemingly unrelated issues, to do with transparency.
- Pavel admits Musk's words can be doubted, but says the US Congress investigation indirectly confirms them. Congress published emails from the pandemic in which European Commission officials pressured Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and others to ban, censor, down-rank, shadow ban and demote inconvenient accounts and narratives.
- The stated purpose was fighting misinformation and conspiracy theories. He says many of those theories later proved at least partially true or worthy of debate (the artificial origins of COVID, the limited nature of anti-COVID measures, the harm of school closures). In his words they were silenced "because they were inconvenient", not because they were untrue.

chunks.heading: Pavel's own case in France and the AI surveillance warning
chunks.text:
- After he was arrested in Paris in 2024 for reasons he says are still unclear, he says the head of French intelligence offered him a secret deal asking him to silence certain political voices. He refused and is still under investigation, facing many years in prison.
- During roughly 3 days of interrogation, a translator appointed by the judge, who had left the Soviet Union in the 1980s to escape limited freedoms, told him she felt like she was "back in the Soviet Union".
- He compares today to the late Soviet era. His parents sent letters and telegrams hoping the KGB would not open them, and surveillance had a human limit: only so many officers and hours in a day.
- AI removes that limit. If privacy is given up, he warns, every message will be monitored and analyzed, every draft, thought and idea scored, and every relationship mapped. The future could be "much darker and more dystopian than the Soviet Union of the '80s".

chunks.heading: Pavel's call to action
chunks.text:
- He says there are no lifeboats and no backup plan, unlike the Titanic's passengers who at least had some. The only option is to fix the ship.
- He urges recognizing the gravity of the situation and acting now, before the loss of freedoms spreads everywhere.
- His platform-level stance, as stated: Telegram refused demands for mass surveillance and censorship even when it was banned in Russia as a result, and it does not disclose private message contents.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains why he built Telegram after losing VK, how it spread with no marketing in places where freedom is at risk, and why he stays neutral on politics. Also covers early privacy features, open-source trust, owning your own crypto stack and the long-term goal of becoming the number one messaging app.

chunks.heading: Pavel's origin story and why Telegram exists
chunks.text:
- Pavel was born in 1984 and was taken to Italy at age four or five, so he experienced both a free-market, free-speech system and a planned-economy, restricted-speech one as a child. He recalls dozens of TV channels and hundreds of ice cream kinds in Italy, versus a few channels of Communist Party content and two or three ice creams in the late Soviet Union.
- He started VK, which became the largest social network in Russia and the post-Soviet states, in 2006.
- In December 2011, with hundreds of thousands protesting in Moscow, the prosecutor's office ordered him to shut down opposition communities on VK. He refused, published a scan of the request, and added a photo of a dog in a hoodie sticking out its tongue as his "official response."
- Armed police then stormed his apartment. He wanted to reach his brother and team and realized no tool was safe, because everything was monitored. He says even WhatsApp sent messages in plain text and added encryption only after Telegram launched.
- He started building Telegram to solve that problem. After Edward Snowden's 2013 revelations he concluded surveillance was a global issue and launched Telegram in 2013.
- With no marketing effort, it spread first in places where privacy and freedoms were at risk.
- He lost VK, selling it below market price after raids and criminal investigations. When Russia demanded encryption keys in 2017-2018, Telegram refused.

chunks.heading: Neutrality and consistent moderation principles
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram will remain a neutral platform that protects everyone regardless of political views or nationality: conservatives and liberals, communists and libertarians, Russians and Ukrainians, Palestinians and Jews. What matters to him is "consistency and the respect to basic human rights."
- He argues people view free speech in a one-sided way. They like it when you protect allies and dislike it when you also protect rivals.
- Examples he gives of equal treatment:
  - During COVID, Telegram protected Black Lives Matter movements and anti-lockdown protesters alike.
  - He recently refused a French police demand to shut down a public channel run by far-left protesters, because it looked legitimate, even though he doesn't agree with communist ideas.
- In Belarus, Telegram refused to censor dissenters. It also polled Belarusian users on who they voted for, and the results differed sharply from the official numbers.
- After China's large DDoS attack on Telegram during the Hong Kong protests, he called it "a badge of honor."
- He says no other social platform has spent as much effort and money defending freedoms in Eastern Europe.

chunks.heading: Privacy and security features Telegram pioneered
chunks.text:
- Pavel says many features now standard in messengers arrived first on Telegram, and he points to stats and infographics on his Telegram channel.
- He lists these:
  - The self-destruct timer, launched in 2013, years before Signal and WhatsApp.
  - An additional passcode lock on the app.
  - Remote deletion of entire chats for all participants, which he says is unique among mass-market messengers. It helps if someone is apprehended by an authoritarian regime.
  - End-to-end encryption for millions of people, rolled out early, with WhatsApp following much later.
- Telegram is open source, so anyone can verify the encryption is what it claims to be. He says WhatsApp isn't open source, and with Signal you can't prove the iOS app matches the GitHub code.

chunks.heading: Balancing encryption with law enforcement
chunks.text:
- Pavel's position is that "messages are sacred." Telegram never discloses a word of private messages.
- If there is a serious concern about an imminent violent crime, and with serious justification and legal documents, Telegram will disclose the IP address or phone number of the suspected user.
- Telegram does this consistently and publishes quarterly transparency reports.
- He says Telegram complied with all binding legal requests it received, and that his French detention (4 days in Paris in 2024) accused him of complicity in users' crimes even though he is a French citizen with a known address.
- He claims Telegram's moderation is more efficient than Instagram, Facebook and Snapchat, based on research the team did in France.
- He alleges that the head of French intelligence asked him to shut down certain channels around the Romanian election. France first denied it, then confirmed meetings but said they were about something else. Telegram takes no side in elections, and Pavel argues for transparency about requests and equal standards for all political players.

chunks.heading: Advice for founders: trust your intuition and experiment
chunks.text:
- Pavel tells young entrepreneurs building for human rights to "trust their own intuition and not be afraid to experiment."
- His encryption example:
  - WhatsApp, Signal, Instagram, Facebook and Google mostly rely on the same encryption algorithm, developed more than 10 years ago with Open Technology Fund money that comes from the US Department of Defense.
  - If something is wrong with it, billions of people depend on a single point of failure.
  - Anyone developing their own standard will face heavy criticism, because cryptography experts tell you to use what everyone else uses.
  - He notes that history has examples of respected experts who turned out to be undercover agents promoting standards that served government goals.
- This is the logic behind Telegram's custom approach to encryption.

chunks.heading: Product positioning and growth vision
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram is the number two global messaging app with more than one billion users. He thinks it has good chances of becoming number one, and could reach three or four billion users within the next 10 years if it keeps doing what it's doing.
- He credits user love to technological superiority, independence, transparency and privacy.
- He keeps innovating on privacy and free speech.
- Differentiator he stresses: users subscribe to channels and sources not manipulated by algorithmic feeds. Most other platforms use non-transparent algorithms that decide what users see, while "on Telegram people are in control."
- He teased an announcement about integrating modern AI technology into Telegram within days.

chunks.heading: Blockchain and TON strategy
chunks.text:
- He says he was a relatively early Bitcoin buyer (2013).
- He calls blockchain "the technology of freedom" that empowers people.
- Telegram designed its own blockchain architecture, the Open Network (TON), to solve scalability. He says it can process hundreds of thousands to millions of transactions, which matters for a platform like Telegram.
- Product uses of the chain:
  - Users can tokenize their usernames and own them directly, so no one, including Telegram, can take a digital identity away.
  - Users can log into Telegram with a blockchain wallet, without relying on a phone number.
- He says he is a big fan of Bitcoin and Toncoin in particular.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov, in his first public appearance, shares VK's scale and a framework for judging how durable a web project is. Services that accumulate useful information and avoid greedy monetization (Wikipedia) last longer than pure communication tools, which are prone to fashion. The rest of the session is Jimmy Wales on SOPA, not Durov's content.

chunks.heading: Wikipedia as the most important digital project
chunks.text:
- Pavel calls Wikipedia "arguably the most important digital project created so far by humankind" and says it is "always underestimated."
- His evidence is personal: 7 out of 10 of his Google searches end on a Wikipedia article, because it holds structured, objective information.
- He contrasts it with VK: VK is profitable with a clear, predictable financial future, while Wikipedia's financial future is not predictable. He still considers Wikipedia the far more important service for the global community.
- He argues that humanity evolves culturally and scientifically (not biologically) by passing knowledge to the next generation, and he sees Wikipedia as the best large-scale effort to accumulate that knowledge. He describes it as the memory section of the "global brain" idea his partner Yuri Milner talks about.
- He says Wikipedia does more to educate young, middle-aged and older people than some governments, so it is unfair that it must raise contributions over several months each year.
- At DLD12 he pledged $1 million to Wikipedia and called on other successful attendees to support it more broadly.

chunks.heading: Information vs. communication: which web products last
chunks.text:
- Pavel sorts web services on an axis from pure information (gathering and structuring knowledge) to pure communication (facilitating interaction between people).
- Services on the information side become more useful over time as they accumulate widely useful, searchable content.
- Services on the communication side are more prone to fashion. His example: "You can use one instant messaging system today and then switch to some other instant messaging tomorrow."
- Facebook sits in between: mainly communication, but with a vast store of profiles, social graph and interest graph.
- His conclusion is that information-heavy products are more robust and longer-term.

chunks.heading: Greed vs. altruism: why users must not feel used
chunks.text:
- Pavel adds a second axis, "greed": how greedy or altruistic users perceive a platform to be. He is explicit that more greed does not mean more profit; in most cases it is the other way around.
- Because most web services rely on user-generated content, users "must not feel offended" or "used" by the service. They must feel the service cares about them.
- Examples he gives of greedy platforms that declined:
  - Classmates.com, one of the first social networks, charged users for sending private messages.
  - StudiVZ, a famous German social network, leaned too hard on advertising and lost user loyalty (he notes several factors were at play).
- He notes Google Plus had no advertisements at the time, which made it the most altruistic of the networks he plotted.
- Combining both axes, he places Wikipedia in the best spot: high on information and highly altruistic, which he links to long-term survival.

chunks.heading: VK's position and growth at the time
chunks.text:
- VK (VKontakte) grew from a website Pavel created five years earlier into the largest social network in Russia and Ukraine and other countries. Its international brand is "vk.com."
- Figures he cites (January 2012): 33 million daily unique visitors, about 77 million monthly actives, and roughly 160 million registered users.
- He cites comScore as ranking it the fourth most viewed website among Europeans, and says it was among the reasons Facebook was not doing well in Russia.
- He notes VK grew fast around the New Year, and that this is "probably one of the reasons why we banned advertisements promoting alcoholic beverages on our network."
- He jokes that VK is the most efficient tool for wasting your time.

chunks.heading: Open internet and regulation (response to the Wikipedia blackout)
chunks.text:
- Pavel says any web project should be grateful that Wikipedia took a stand on SOPA/PIPA.
- He admits US laws did not directly affect VK, and that VK had no real copyright problems in the Russian legal system. He still says such a law would affect VK "in some future" if it passed.
- He agrees with the idea that US internet regulation inspires laws elsewhere, so poorly designed laws are bad for the industry everywhere.

chunks.heading: Entertainment industry and the VCR analogy
chunks.text:
- Pavel recounts learning the day before that 30 years earlier the movie industry opposed the VCR, with claims it would destroy the industry and cost huge numbers of jobs. The video cassette business went on to yield huge profits for movie makers.
- He argues the internet is similar: a disruptive technology that "will eventually result in creating more profit for movie makers in case they learn how to use it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains why Telegram started from "WhatsApp sucks" product gaps (no cross-device, limited media, no privacy), how a bot platform created an app-like ecosystem, and why he stays bootstrapped with a 15-person team. He also covers market-specific content blocking and why growth numbers should be compared by app age.

chunks.heading: Why Telegram exists: other messengers "suck"
chunks.text:
Pavel built Telegram because he thinks existing messengers are poor products. His case against WhatsApp (as of 2015):
- If the phone dies or the battery runs out, you lose access to your messages.
- No real cross-device sync.
- Limits on sending documents and large media.
- Many limitations in group chats.
- It is not private.

He says "it doesn't matter how many other messaging apps are out there if all of them suck." He had been a fan of WhatsApp a few years earlier, but changed his mind.

chunks.heading: Privacy as a product and retention advantage
chunks.text:
- He ties privacy to real harm. A friend in Russia was shown a printout of her WhatsApp messages at a police department, which he says was used to try to blackmail her.
- Business users are the most exposed, because their information is more valuable and they can be blackmailed or compromised.
- He says users stay with Telegram because they trust that messages can't be intercepted. It is one of several differentiators.
- In its first two years Telegram "haven't disclosed a single byte of data to third parties including governments," and he says that "was not easy."
- On terrorists using the platform, he argues that the right to privacy matters more than the fear of bad things like terrorism. Groups such as ISIS would switch to another channel if one were insecure, and open-source encrypted apps already exist. He doesn't think Telegram should feel guilty and says it is doing the right thing by protecting users' privacy.

chunks.heading: Bot platform as an ecosystem and app store
chunks.text:
- The bot platform launched in June 2015. Third-party developers use a simple API to create a bot, a "user" you talk to on Telegram, with a machine handling messages on the other side.
- At about three months old, categories included dating, education and productivity.
- He had learned the day before that one of the most successful bots received an eight-digit acquisition attempt.
- He compares bots to apps for Telegram, and thinks developers may end up building real businesses on it.
- Planned next step: a payment API so bot developers can accept money from users inside Telegram.
- Advertising: some third-party bots already send ads, and there is a third-party agency for it. He is "not a big fan of ads", but users opt in to receive messages from those bots, so it is allowed.

chunks.heading: Content moderation as a business decision
chunks.text:
- Telegram blocks porn bots in markets where porn is prohibited, such as Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia. Blocked porn websites were reappearing as bots on Telegram, bringing in users the team didn't want.
- He says it is a business decision, not a secret government deal, and doesn't want Telegram perceived as a source of porn.
- He points out Apple, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and Google do the same.
- Hard line: Telegram would never block a bot that criticises governments or supports opposition activity.

chunks.heading: Growth and engagement metrics
chunks.text:
- Over 60 million users. Messages delivered daily grew from 1 billion in February 2015 to 10 billion announced the previous month, and over 12 billion by the day of the interview.
- He reads the jump as users switching: people who installed Telegram as a backup app now use it as their primary messenger.
- He says people tend to start their day in their messaging app, and messaging is "probably the biggest thing going on in social media in this decade."
- He dislikes announcing user numbers. Media compare Telegram's 60-100 million with WhatsApp's 800-900 million, ignoring that Telegram was two years old and WhatsApp over six.

chunks.heading: Super-app strategy: cautious about the Asian model
chunks.text:
- On WeChat-style services (ordering cars, goods, pizza), he says "yes and no."
- That model needs very high market penetration and social relevance everywhere. Telegram is number one in a few markets but lacks the dominance WeChat has in China, Line in Japan or KakaoTalk in Korea.
- Telegram will experiment with payments, bots and third-party apps built on top of it, but doesn't see itself going the full super-app route in the near future.

chunks.heading: Staying independent, lean and nomadic
chunks.text:
- No outside funding for Telegram. He prefers independence and says "there's more than market shares and revenue streams."
- He has enough money to last a long time and says Telegram will keep doing "what we think is right."
- The team is about 15 people. They rent houses short term around the world (Finland in summer, Paris in spring) and build together there.
- Design and customer support are outsourced to Eastern and Southern Europe.
- He sold his VKontakte stake just before the Ukraine events and the currency fall, and says the company's value is now probably three or four times lower. He calls himself very lucky on timing.
- He plays down Russia as a market. It is roughly Telegram's number seven by size, and he already owned the Russian market with VKontakte, so it is "not a new challenge."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2014 SVTV interview, Durov explains why VK needn't chase global markets, how Telegram grew out of a nonprofit research effort to combine speed with security, and why builders must protect privacy. Mostly product and privacy philosophy, light on growth tactics.

chunks.heading: VK vs. Facebook: positioning and international expansion
chunks.text:
- Pavel thinks Zuckerberg "still underestimates VK in some ways" and suspects he doesn't use VK much.
- VK is not a global Facebook. Several technologies appeared first on VK and later on Facebook.
- VK is popular in Russia, Ukraine and other post-Soviet countries because it is faster, easier to use and has more of the functionality that population wants.
- Going global is not a goal to spend money on. VK translates the product into other languages and sees whether it catches on. If it happens naturally, good; if not, he won't worry.
- On an IPO, the VK IPO was cancelled after Facebook's IPO sent a bad market signal. Market conditions now look good, but he says it is too early to decide.

chunks.heading: Music licensing and copyright on VK
chunks.text:
- Pavel disputes that VK is an illegal download service. Users can't download music or video on VK; there is only a streaming service.
- The service is DMCA compliant. Rights holders can send a takedown request, the item is deleted and the user cannot upload it again.
- VK was negotiating with Sony Music on ways for rights holders to earn money from the streaming service. He was optimistic about a solution within several months.
- He confirms this amounts to building a Spotify-like music service.

chunks.heading: Telegram: origin and product design
chunks.text:
- Telegram started as a nonprofit research project, built around one question: why must messaging be either fast and easy or secure, never both?
- A dedicated team (his brother led the research and created a new data protocol) built a messenger he claims is faster than the fastest on the market, with strong encryption including end-to-end.
- The project had been going for over a year.
- It is not a business project or an investment vehicle. It is nonprofit and open source, closer to a set of technologies plus apps (e.g. on Android) than a company.
- He says it won't compete with VK. Telegram is a messenger, not a social network, with different demographics and no tie to Russia.

chunks.heading: Telegram's differentiators vs. WhatsApp
chunks.text:
- **Security:** "military grade" security. He says WhatsApp traffic can be monitored and the messages easily decrypted. With Telegram, from what they've seen, that is impossible, especially with end-to-end encryption.
- **Infrastructure:** decentralized, with servers spread around the world. Users connect to the closest one to talk with local friends.
- **Openness:** the project is open source and fully documented, and the API is an open platform anyone can use to build their own secure messenger.
- **Speed and cloud:** fast and cloud-based, so messages are accessible from several devices at once. He contrasts this with WhatsApp, where you have to choose one device.
- **Price:** completely free.

chunks.heading: Government pressure, shareholders and Telegram's separation from VK
chunks.text:
- VK would have included Telegram's encryption, but some shareholders would not have liked that. Pavel says both major shareholders have ties to the government.
- He says those shareholders made clear they don't want this kind of encryption project. He thinks encryption could be "perceived in the wrong way", which is part of why Telegram is kept separate.
- He sees no direct connection between himself and the government, and says he is doing useful things for the country, such as developing Russian IT as an example for the younger generation.
- He called the April traffic charges a public relations campaign: every major Russian TV channel ran a story, then footage was reviewed and the claims fell apart.
- He took about two months off during that period to figure out what to do next.
- On data requests: if you use end-to-end encryption, there is no data to hand over, and even Telegram's own system administrator can't access private data. He invites people to review the open-source algorithms and check for themselves.
- Telegram had received no requests so far, despite the fact that a Boston bomber was a VK user.

chunks.heading: Privacy, surveillance and transparency
chunks.text:
- Pavel says the situation is similar almost everywhere. The difference in Eastern Europe is that governments are open about wanting data, while in the US governments claim privacy is sacred and then it turns out it isn't.
- **Transparency first:** society needs to understand what is collected and why, then debate whether it accepts "big brother", before deciding on a solution.
- **Engineers' responsibility:** it is on IT businessmen and engineers to build technologies that make total surveillance impossible.
- He calls privacy a sacred right, guaranteed by most European constitutions and, he believes, in the US. Russia's constitution protects private correspondence unless a court decides otherwise.
- He rejects terrorism as a pretext for violating everyone's privacy. His argument is statistical: more people die from everyday accidents, like slipping on a wet floor in a bathroom, than from terrorist attacks. By that logic, governments could justify installing cameras in bathrooms for safety.
- He thinks the most popular private-communication companies, above all WhatsApp, should introduce transparent algorithms. The field was neglected for years: "security was number 10" behind new products, which he calls wrong.
- On Snowden, he says Telegram offered him a job doing privacy work. He calls Snowden one of his personal heroes for sacrificing a large part of his life to tell people they were being spied on. He had not met him.
- He sees Telegram as a "fighting project" to push more companies to protect user privacy, including voice over IP, social networking and other tools.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains Telegram's creator-first model: contextual ads with no personal-data targeting, 50% ad revenue sharing, free tools for merchants, and blockchain-based payments and tokenized usernames. He argues platform success belongs to creators and developers, so the platform should give back and keep rules fair for everyone.

chunks.heading: Telegram's positioning: freedom, no ad-data selling, and sharing revenue
chunks.text:
Pavel frames Telegram around freedom: a logo (paper airplane) that "symbolizes freedom to move in three dimensions," freedom to communicate privately and to express yourself publicly. He says Telegram allows more freedom to third-party developers than any other major communication app, and that it integrated blockchain more deeply than any big social platform.

Scale he cites:
- 900 million monthly active users.
- 360 million of them interact with mini apps each month (stated as "300 UH 60 million" in the transcript, read here as 360 million).
- Telegram is the sixth most used and sixth most downloaded mobile app.
- Later this year Telegram plans to start suggesting mini apps and chatbots to users, which he expects to lift mini-app/chatbot users to over 700 million monthly.

How he says Telegram differs from the other top-five apps:
- It does not use personal data to target ads and does not sell it to advertisers. All ads are context-based.
- It does not put algorithmic feeds between creators and their audience, and does not shadow-ban creators for posting their own promotions.
- It shares revenue. He credits Telegram's success to app developers, community leaders, content creators, sticker artists and users who invite friends, and says users are "equal to us."

chunks.heading: Ad revenue sharing: 50% to channel owners, paid on blockchain
chunks.text:
- Last month (March 2024) Telegram launched what Pavel calls one of the most generous revenue-sharing models in social media history: 50% of proceeds from ads shown in broadcast channels goes to the channel owners.
- First withdrawals were happening on the day of the keynote, and many people had already earned money.
- Ad payments and withdrawals run exclusively on the TON blockchain. He notes this puts a market of "several hundred million dollar" today, and potentially tens of billions in ad spend, "on the rails of blockchain."
- Next step: optional revenue sharing for large public group chats (many-to-many communities), also with half of proceeds going to owners.
- Within a few weeks: revenue sharing for tips to creators, which he calls a multi-billion-dollar market. Purchases are constrained by Apple and Google in-app purchase mechanisms, but withdrawals will be on blockchain (TON).
- His stated rationale is moral as much as commercial: the earlier model where a platform "operated almost like a digital slavery should be over," even if it "may not make much sense in terms of commercial interest of Telegram."

chunks.heading: Merchants and digital goods
chunks.text:
- For several years Telegram has let developers and merchants sell physical goods and services on the platform free of charge.
- It has integrated 40 payment providers, such as Stripe, so users can easily buy from mini apps and bots.
- Next stage: a no-code store setup so simple merchants can open a shop and accept payments without coding.
- In a few weeks: users will be able to buy digital goods and services from app developers. Again limited by Apple/Google in-app purchase rules, but withdrawals will happen on blockchain, with another revenue-sharing model he calls one of the most generous in history.

chunks.heading: Tokenizing usernames and anonymous numbers on TON
chunks.text:
- Telegram was the first social platform to tokenize its entire username space, via the Fragment platform. He says that market reached $350 million in sales.
- Users can own a username directly, sell it, auction it, and attach multiple usernames to an account.
- Fairness example: Pavel tried to win a nice username for a famous friend in a Fragment auction and lost. "The smart contract... doesn't care whether it's the CEO and owner of Telegram."
- Telegram was also the first major platform to let users sign up and log in with a blockchain wallet, using "anonymous numbers," NFTs on TON that work like usernames.
- Anonymous numbers had utility, unlike "monkey NFTs," and their price rose 33 times. He says many people made money buying and reselling them, which he did not expect.

chunks.heading: Next step: stickers and emoji as NFTs
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram believes in "socially relevant NFTs" deeply integrated into culture and communication, ones seen "tens of billions of times" that can spread virally.
- The next step is tokenizing Telegram stickers. His example is a smoking-duck sticker made by one of the platform's most talented sticker artists. It got "hundreds of millions of views at least" and became a meme outside Telegram. He suggests owning it as an NFT from the start might have rivalled the anonymous-number price rise.
- Stickers are shared more than 700 billion times a month on Telegram.
- He says emoji could become NFTs too, and sticker and emoji sets might even become their own meme coins.

chunks.heading: Why TON, and Telegram's lean team
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram relies on TON because of scale: it needs a chain able to process tens or hundreds of millions of transactions, and TON set a record for transactions per minute last year. He also cites fast transactions and low fees.
- He says the logo and its resemblance to a paper airplane are not the reason.
- Pavel states that Telegram runs with a small headcount of around 60 people (this is attributed to him by Paolo Ardoino later in the talk, so treat the figure as secondhand).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains how Telegram grew to 100M monthly users and 15B daily messages with no marketing budget, relying on organic word of mouth. He shows how open APIs, bots and channels let Telegram add capability without adding complexity, and why short release cycles matter.

chunks.heading: Telegram's origin and the lightweight, secure protocol (2013)
chunks.text:
- Pavel traces Telegram to 2013, when the team built a custom lightweight encrypted data protocol that could send messages securely over the weakest network connections.
- To keep Telegram "the fastest means of communication" everywhere, they set up a distributed server infrastructure all over the world.
- Secret chats, also launched in 2013, were "an instant hit" because they offered encryption and self-destruct timers, which mattered in the wake of Edward Snowden's revelations.
- He frames this as groundwork: security and speed came first, and later features were built on top.

chunks.heading: Letting usage lead product direction (2014)
chunks.text:
- In 2014 Telegram reached broader audiences. Pavel noticed users loved cross-device synchronization and built-in cloud features.
- Users began moving activities from email and other messengers to Telegram, using it for business tasks as well as family and friends.
- The team responded by adding features that supported that use:
  - Instant search across millions of messages in chat history.
  - Strong laptop and tablet support.
  - Unlimited, very fast file transfer.
  - Massive group chats, kept manageable with replies, mentions and hashtags.
- His claim: all of this was added "without making the app more complicated." He says Telegram is still the easiest and simplest messaging app on the market.

chunks.heading: Keeping the app simple by building a platform
chunks.text:
- Pavel's answer to "how do we add features without adding complexity?" is to build a platform and give third parties open APIs, so they create specific tools for specific audience needs.
- Telegram has been open from the start: in 2013 its API was 100% open and free, and he calls it probably the only massively popular messaging app with that property.
- In 2015 the team opened the bot platform. Third parties could build small apps inside Telegram using the familiar message interface as the UI.
- Thousands of developers used Telegram's social graph. Bots cover gaming, dating, custom services and integrating third-party applications.
- Forbes example: Forbes launched a Telegram bot letting users subscribe to news categories and search its database. It took Forbes only 3 days to set up and needs no extra human resources to maintain.

chunks.heading: Growth: 100 million users with zero marketing
chunks.text:
- Telegram announced 100 million active users, up from 62 million announced in May of the prior year.
- Pavel says 350 thousand new users sign up every day (the transcript renders it as "350").
- All growth is "100% organic": "we have a zero marketing budget" and spend nothing on ads or other user acquisition.
- Growth comes from people recommending Telegram to friends and colleagues as a more efficient, reliable communication tool.
- Telegram has users in more than 200 countries, with at least a few million users in many of them.
- Engagement: 15 billion messages delivered daily, a huge increase over the previous year. He reads this as people using Telegram as their primary communication tool, not just one of several messengers.

chunks.heading: Channels: direct broadcast and why creators switch
chunks.text:
- After bots launched, Pavel saw media and bloggers using them to broadcast customized messages and news to mass audiences.
- In September 2015 Telegram launched channels, a tool to publicly broadcast to an unlimited number of recipients, giving media and businesses a direct line to readers and customers.
- Scale cited: some channels have reached over 100 million recipients, and channels are viewed 400 million times a day. BBC has used channels since September to reach over 300,000 users, and the Pope's Lent messages were reported to reach thousands of members the same day.
- Why bloggers move: it creates a direct relationship with the reader. Pavel, who founded a social network 20 years earlier, says in traditional social networks "your voice could be easily lost in the chaos of news feeds," while in a messaging app it is "much more straightforward and direct."
- Channels are widely used in emerging markets as well.

chunks.heading: Release cadence and the bet on messaging
chunks.text:
- Pavel believes in short production cycles and tries to launch new features at least every month. He says the update released that day was "literally built" within the last week.
- Each update is one in a continuing series, aimed at improving channels and bots.
- His forecast: "this could be the decade of messaging and things, products and services built on top of messaging."

chunks.heading: Privacy stance: Apple versus the US government
chunks.text:
- Asked about Apple and the US government, Pavel says he would "definitely side with Tim Cook."
- His argument: building tools to unlock a PIN-locked iPhone slightly raises the risk that a stolen phone's private photos and data could be used for blackmail.
- He calls this "extremely dangerous" because hundreds of millions of people use iPhones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pavel Durov explains how Telegram grew to 100M monthly users on organic referrals, with a 15-person distributed team, by removing limits rivals imposed and adding features through open platforms. He also covers staying independent, monetization options, and moving fast without a rigid roadmap.

chunks.heading: Telegram's product principles: simplicity, open platforms, speed
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram's edge is being "the most easy to use, the fastest and the most secure" messaging service, and that focusing on the best service for customers is what drove growth.
- He pitches Telegram against rivals on removing limitations. It had multi-device sync, persistent and instantly searchable history (usable "as you use email"), file sharing of any size, and 1,000-member group chats against 100 elsewhere.
- He says it also works reliably on weak connections.
- His design question is "how do we add features without adding complexity".
- The iPhone app has three tabs versus WhatsApp's five.
- His answer is open platforms for third-party developers. Users who don't need a feature never see it.
- Stickers are the example. They launched early 2015 as a user-generated platform. Business users see none, while sticker fans can upload and share packs. He says it "unleashed" creativity.
- On features, he says Telegram ships a major update on every platform every month or month and a half.
- He declines to promise specific features such as phone calls. The roadmap is "fluid" and a small team keeps flexibility to reprioritise when a trend appears.
- He cites voice messaging as a current focus.

chunks.heading: Growth: 100 million users with no marketing spend
chunks.text:
- Telegram announced 100 million monthly active users in February 2016, up from roughly 40-50 million a year earlier. He says growth is on every continent except Africa.
- It was at zero about two and a half years before, while WhatsApp already had hundreds of millions of users. He argues it is easier to grow from 100 million than from zero.
- Growth is organic. He says "every day 350,000 people sign up for telegram without any activity from our party. We don't spend anything."
- Growth relies solely on users telling friends to switch.
- He disputes the idea that network effects lock users in. People already use several messaging apps, one each for friends, co-workers and family, so he doubts a single winner will emerge.
- He says users "are eager to switch to a superior alternative". A large share came from WhatsApp and Facebook.
- Outages help. When WhatsApp was blocked in Brazil, a few million people signed up for Telegram that day. He treats that traffic as non-organic and does not rely on it.

chunks.heading: Running a 15-person team at 15 billion messages a day
chunks.text:
- Telegram delivers 15 billion messages a day with a core engineering team of 15.
- To keep that going he leans on scripts and "artificial intelligence rather than real human labor" to run infrastructure.
- He credits experience from scaling VKontakte, which at times reached similar metrics.
- The team is distributed and moves country every two to four months.
  - He says three months is ideal.
  - The first week in a new place is wasted getting used to it.
  - Shorter stays distract the team.
- They rent a big house or office plus nearby apartments.
- Travel produces product ideas. In Indonesia (November-December 2015) they saw people using Telegram differently and improved functionality as a result.
- Telegram keeps small offices in Berlin and a legal and accounting office in London. In summer they prefer the Finnish lake district.
- The infrastructure is distributed too:
  - Data sits in multiple data centres worldwide.
  - Cloud data is encrypted with a key split into parts held in different jurisdictions.
  - No single jurisdiction can regulate the data.
- He avoided basing in London after David Cameron's remarks on messaging apps giving law enforcement access. He would not invest in an office only to find the place "inconsistent with our mission".

chunks.heading: Origins: from student websites to VKontakte
chunks.text:
- Pavel started at St Petersburg State University by building websites for his department, sharing exam materials.
- The site grew to the whole university (about 20,000 students).
- It then spread to other prestigious Russian universities, all while he was under 20.
- He decided a decentralised social network was needed rather than a portal. He launched VKontakte in 2006 and used his earlier projects as the initial user base.
- Registration later opened to other post-soviet countries and to people with no university degree.
- It reached tens of millions of users within a few years.
- Early on the Russian government paid little attention to the internet. He says Putin didn't use it, so regulating it made little sense to officials.
- After the protests of December 2011, new laws came in and government-friendly funds and oligarchs began buying internet companies.

chunks.heading: Control, pressure and the loss of VKontakte
chunks.text:
- Requests from the authorities came as formal signed documents. They asked him to block Alexei Navalny's opposition community and to hand over personal data of Ukrainian protesters. He publicly refused.
- He argued that blocking one network made no sense because the activity would just move to other platforms.
- Armed police came to his door in December 2011 but were not authorised to arrest him.
- That episode planted the Telegram idea. He couldn't be sure his communication with his brother was not being monitored, and that led them to think about an encryption protocol.
- Ownership was the weakness.
  - He and his partners and seed investors originally controlled about 60%.
  - After the investors sold, a fund close to the government secretly bought 48%.
  - Pavel was left with only 12%, so he could not influence his own dismissal as CEO.
  - Shareholders fired him partly to remove the risk his refusals created for them.
- He was in the US when it happened and did not return.
- He says running Telegram from Russia was not possible given the legal framework on private data.
- He sold his Russian company stake at the right moment, before the market crashed, and now funds Telegram himself.

chunks.heading: Funding and business model
chunks.text:
- Telegram is financed from his personal cash, with no outside investment.
- He has received many offers from funds and big companies, including the Sequoia type of deal done with WhatsApp. He says he doesn't need outside money now and hopes never to.
- His stated hope is that Telegram can come up with a sustainable business model and cover its expenses.
- He calls it a chance to "give back to society" by keeping Telegram free and independent.
- Runway depends on growth speed. Faster growth raises the monthly burn rate, which may force monetisation sooner.
- At the current growth rate he thinks he can manage "another few years".
- A fallback to buy time would be investment or a loan.
- He wants Telegram independent of big companies. He doesn't rule out a sale in extreme circumstances such as a financial crisis, but he says it is not the plan.
- Monetisation ideas he raises:
  - Advertising does not fit private messaging, but public channels could carry ads, and some media already insert them.
  - A revenue-sharing model for channels is possible.
  - A payment platform for bots, letting third-party services take money from users, where Telegram could take a small cut.
- WhatsApp's move to free and its business services copy Telegram, which was always free. He says its bot and business features were already on Telegram.

chunks.heading: Competition, copying and encryption
chunks.text:
- On WhatsApp he says it copied Telegram's features: a desktop app, end-to-end encryption, and bigger group limits (50 to 100, while Telegram went from 200 to 1,000).
- He sees that as a benefit, since a broader market gets better service. He once wrote a blog post, "how to predict WhatsApp features".
- Jan Koum had said in 2013 that Pavel "knows how to copy great products". Pavel counters that the last two years of WhatsApp's evolution have been copying Telegram.
- On encryption and terrorist use:
  - Terrorists use many apps, and Telegram did not invent end-to-end encryption (Apple's iMessage had it).
  - Any popular app will see more illegal use.
  - Telegram cannot read private messages.
  - Backdoors would not work. Telegram is open source, so tampering would be noticed.
  - Bad actors would move to another app, and building one costs only tens of thousands of dollars.
  - The result would be less security for ordinary users while the problem remains.
  - He sees the tool as neutral, like a car maker building the best car.
- Public channels are different. They can be reported, and Telegram takes them down. It blocked around 600 Islamic State channels after the Paris attacks.
- He admits Telegram is "probably not" doing enough, since it is a small team still building tools to automate this.
- He argues that how societies trade privacy against security is for each society to decide, but his Russian experience makes him sceptical of "big brother" moves.
- He holds a free-market, decentralised view. He thinks large hierarchical organisations are inefficient in the 21st century, and that centralisation breeds corruption and inefficiency.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov recounts the FBI's 2016 attempt to pressure him and bribe a Telegram engineer, and explains why jurisdiction matters for a privacy-first company. He argues that mission-driven products need independence from governments and platform owners, and commits to speaking out regardless of personal risk.

chunks.heading: Why Pavel left the US out of Telegram's plans: the FBI approach in May 2016
chunks.text:
- In May 2016, during a one-week trip to America, the FBI tried to influence Pavel and bribe a Telegram engineer to make Telegram less secure.
- Neither of them is a US citizen, so they "could afford to refuse their offers" and Pavel told the public about the attempts.
- He points to a legal tool, the "gag order": US authorities can demand a company plant a backdoor in its app and also forbid it from telling the public, on pain of jail.
- If the team was pressured this much in one week, he asks what US-based tech companies face every day, and how a privacy-oriented company can operate permanently from America.

chunks.heading: Why jurisdiction matters for a privacy product
chunks.text:
- Pavel's view is that a legal system being "open" does not help when gag orders are secret: "we would never even know if things went wrong."
- He treats Edward Snowden's revelations as confirmation of "some of the worst fears."
- The practical lesson he draws: where the company and its founders are based determines whether they can refuse pressure and speak publicly about it.
- Non-US citizens on a short trip could say no and disclose; US citizens could have been silenced.

chunks.heading: Distrust of government-funded "privacy advocates"
chunks.text:
- He cites the article's facts as confirming a long-held fear: some famous, vocal US-based influencers in the cryptography world are sponsored by the US government to push its agencies' agenda.
- Known precedent he names: the NSA infiltrating RSA.
- He believes collaboration between US agencies and influential "privacy advocates" runs "much deeper" than the known cases.
- Implication he draws: don't take security advice or reputation signals at face value; check who funds the source.

chunks.heading: Platform dependence as a structural weakness
chunks.text:
- Telegram depends on Google and Apple for mobile operating systems, and both are US-based, which makes protecting privacy "really hard."
- Pavel says he sees "no easy recipe or solution."
- His wish: huge companies like Apple and Google become independent of any government that can distort their founders' mission, and he jokes they might "start their own countries."

chunks.heading: Pavel's stance on resisting pressure
chunks.text:
- He will keep building Telegram and protecting users, "even if that will require speaking out under gag orders."
- He acknowledges it could get him into trouble, as it did when he lived in Russia.
- He says it is the only way he can imagine going forward, so he has no regrets: "It's all worth it because of you guys – the millions of users who entrusted their private data to Telegram."
- He frames user trust (millions of users) as the reason the personal risk is worth taking.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains why prosecutions in Iran and Russia don't hurt Telegram: the company has no legal presence there and severs any local link (like the outsourced spam contractor Telegraf) so regulators have nothing to target. He argues restrictive laws in an open, connected world mostly hurt the countries that pass them.

chunks.heading: Why Iran and Russia charges don't affect Telegram or Pavel
chunks.text:
- Pavel says the charges "won't" affect Telegram or him personally.
- Travel bans cost him little. He has no ties to Iran. Russia is harder, since he is ethnic Russian (with a St. Kitts passport) and his parents live there, but he calls missing visits "a small price to pay considering the matters at stake."
- Telegram has no legal presence in either country, so there is nothing for those governments to pressure.

chunks.heading: How Telegram cut its last link to Russia
chunks.text:
- The last link was "Telegraf", a Saint-Petersburg company that Telegram outsourced spam fighting to (the spam came from Russia and Iran).
- Telegraf mattered more in the early days, when Pavel lived in Russia. Its role shrank after he left in 2014 with the core team.
- Telegram terminated the contract in July 2017, after Russian authorities threatened to block Telegram in June. Telegraf let go all its employees and changed owner.
- When Russian authorities sent warnings to the London office in September, there was nobody in their jurisdiction to target, "not even Russian spam moderators."
- The tactic: keep operations, people and contracts outside any jurisdiction that can be used as leverage.

chunks.heading: Restrictive laws hurt the country that passes them
chunks.text:
- Pavel argues: "it's 2017, and the world is open and connected." Archaic laws that limit freedoms mostly kill the passing country's own economy.
- Example: in recent years Google, Oracle and Microsoft (Skype) shut down development offices in Russia, and many smaller companies followed.

chunks.heading: Iran as a market
chunks.text:
- Iran is not blocking Telegram. For the last few years about 40 million Iranians have used it to communicate securely and get news from independent channels.
- Instagram and WhatsApp are also accessible there, while almost all major internet services were blocked several years ago (some still are).
- Pavel sees Iran as becoming "more open and market-driven," though he wants a more IT-friendly prosecutor of Tehran.
- Contrasts: Chinese and North Koreans have far fewer freedoms, and Saudi Arabia throttled Telegram's traffic until recently.

chunks.heading: Stance on legal pressure
chunks.text:
- Telegram serves users in Russia and Iran from "places that respect freedom," and hopes to open offices there someday, as other IT companies could.
- "We don't care if specific countries press charges against us for defending the privacy of our users."
- Policy: Telegram is always ready to cut all personal and business links to a place so it has no leverage over the company.
- Blocking a service in a territory doesn't always work, as he showed in an earlier post about China.
