- His long-term view: "freedom and privacy will prevail," and those who want to return to the 1930s "will find themselves on the wrong side of history."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains Telegram's stance on free speech: it resists political censorship pressure but blocks channels that promote violence. The post sets a simple rule of thumb for moderating public channels, useful for anyone running a platform with user-generated content.

chunks.heading: Freedom of speech as a core value
chunks.text:
- Pavel treats freedom of speech as a human right Telegram defends alongside privacy: "You already know Telegram has your back when it comes to privacy. Another human right we feel passionately about is the freedom of speech."
- He says Telegram has defended it for 11 years (as of 2017): first in Russia, then globally.
- In some countries Telegram is the only popular platform for independent sources of information.
- Example he gives: in Iran the BBC is blocked, yet its @bbcpersian Telegram channel has been active for years and attracted almost a million followers.
- He notes there are thousands of large Telegram channels critical of their governments.

chunks.heading: Refusing political censorship
chunks.text:
- Pavel states that "Telegram has never yielded to pressure from officials who wanted us to perform political censorship."
- Telegram's stance is presented as a long-standing, consistent position held across countries, not a one-off.
- The product's value in restrictive markets comes from this: users and independent media can reach audiences that state-controlled or blocked platforms cannot.

chunks.heading: Where the line is: Pavel's rule of thumb
chunks.text:
- He describes the line as "pretty straightforward" and applies it whenever moderating public channels.
- Acceptable:
  - Criticizing local authorities
  - Challenging the status quo
  - Engaging in political debate
- Not acceptable:
  - Promoting violence
  - Calling for actions that can harm innocent people
- The test is about harm and violence, not about whether the speech is political or unpopular with governments.

chunks.heading: Rules for channel admins and enforcement
chunks.text:
- Telegram's Terms of Service prohibit publicly promoting violence in any form. Channel admins must respect this.
- Enforcement scale he cites: in October 2017 alone, Telegram blocked over 8,500 channels related to terrorism, with more stats published in @isiswatch.
- Enforcement applies to public channels. The post frames the rules as applying to promotion of violence, not to political content.

chunks.heading: Case study: the Iranian vandalism-contest channel
chunks.text:
- Pavel describes an Iranian channel that urged members to throw stones into windows of public buildings and vehicles (schools, temples, buses) and film it.
- His process before blocking:
  1. Telegram contacted the channel admins.
  2. It asked them to stop the "vandalism contest."
  3. The admins ignored the request and escalated.
- The escalation: the channel launched another competition urging its 100K+ users to burn mosques by throwing Molotov cocktails into them and film it.
- Outcome: "we were left with no other options but to block their channel."
- Takeaway: Telegram tries direct contact and a warning first, and blocks only when admins refuse to stop and escalate the calls for violence.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains the product philosophy behind Telegram's feature letting every user delete any message in a private chat for both parties, at any time. The core argument: encryption alone doesn't give users real control over their data, because copies sit in other people's inboxes forever.

chunks.heading: Message deletion: control over your own digital footprint
chunks.text: Pavel announced on 2019-03-24 that every Telegram user can now delete any message in a private conversation from both sides. Core idea: you should have control over data you created, even when it sits in someone else's inbox.

chunks.heading: The problem Pavel is solving
chunks.text:
- Pavel has used private messaging for 23 years and built his own services for 16.
- Over 10-20 years, each person exchanges millions of messages with thousands of people. Most of those logs sit in other people's inboxes, outside the sender's reach.
- Relationships end, but chat histories with ex-friends and ex-colleagues "remain available forever."
- He expects the volume of private data held by chat partners to "easily quadruple" within a few decades.
- Despite progress in encryption and privacy, he argues users have "very little actual control of our data" because they cannot go back and erase things for other people.

chunks.heading: The risk he names
chunks.text:
- An old, forgotten message can be taken out of context and used against you decades later.
- His example: a hasty text sent to a girlfriend in school could come back in 2030 when you decide to run for mayor.

chunks.heading: What shipped
chunks.text:
- Any user can delete any message in a private conversation from both sides.
- It works regardless of who sent the message and when it was sent.
- Users can wipe out a whole conversation from both sides.
- "No trace will be left on either side."

chunks.heading: How he weighs the trade-off
chunks.text:
- He acknowledges concerns about misuse of the feature and about the permanence of chat histories.
- The team "thought carefully through those issues" and still concluded that control over your own digital footprint "should be paramount."
- He sets user control above the objection that deletion could be abused.

chunks.heading: Product principle
chunks.text:
- Privacy is framed as ownership of your own history, not just encryption in transit.
- He tests the feature on himself: looking through his own inbox, he finds little he would want to delete, yet says he feels "truly free and in control" for the first time in 23 years of private messaging.
- The value of the feature lies in having the option, even if it is rarely used.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov describes 15 years without alcohol, caffeine, meat, pills or fast food, plus escalating restrictions and a water fast. He frames self-restraint as a tool for productivity, clarity of thought and self-discipline, which he ties to better product management for Telegram.

chunks.heading: Self-restraint as a productivity and willpower system
chunks.text:
- Pavel calls himself "a big believer in self-restraint."
- For the 15 years before this 2019 post he had no alcohol, caffeine, meat, pills or fast food.
- He credits this with health results: he had a fever only once in 15 years and "typically, I just don't get ill."

chunks.heading: Escalating diet restrictions to train discipline
chunks.text:
- About a year before the post he added more limits: no gluten, no dairy, no eggs, no fructose.
- His stated aims were higher productivity and clarity of thought, plus training willpower and self-discipline.
- In May 2019 he cut his diet to fish and seafood only.
- He recommends that diet for boosting productivity if you have daily access to fresh wild-caught fish.

chunks.heading: The "seagan" evolutionary argument
chunks.text:
- Farmed meat and agricultural products entered the human diet only about 15,000 years ago.
- Wild fish cooked on fire is something our ancestors "evolved to consume throughout the last million of years."
- Humans needed daily water, so they lived near rivers and lakes.
- He therefore finds a seagan (fish and seafood) diet makes "much more sense" than veganism or rawism from an evolutionary perspective.

chunks.heading: Ice-cold swimming as a procrastination cure
chunks.text:
- Every winter in Finland or Switzerland he swims in ice-cold water to improve willpower.
- Having stayed for minutes in a lake with a thin layer of ice on top makes you "less likely to procrastinate when it comes to starting on a boring but necessary project."
- The logic is that doing something deliberately hard makes starting unpleasant work easier.

chunks.heading: Water fasting for clarity and product work
chunks.text:
- In the month of the post he went further and consumed no food at all.
- He had been on a water fast for 6 days and felt great.
- He says zero food consumption improves clarity of thought, and he got many things done on the product-management side.
- He argues fasting lets the digestive system "clean and reboot" and frees the immune system from constantly clearing incoming food.
- Hunter-gatherer ancestors went long periods without food, so he believes the body expects a break in consumption at least once a year.
- He notes most religions have a fasting tradition because it is "healthy and necessary both for the body and the mind."

chunks.heading: Motivation: Telegram users come first
chunks.text:
- He accepts he may lose some muscle mass from fasting.
- He considers the trade worthwhile if he comes up with great new ideas for Telegram during the fast, since they would benefit "all of the millions of Telegram users."
- He states that making users' lives more enjoyable "has been and will be my number one priority."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov argues that recurring WhatsApp backdoors are evidence of a surveillance-friendly owner, not accidents, and that Telegram's clean record in comparable complexity proves security is achievable. The essay is mostly a trust and positioning argument for Telegram, with little on growth mechanics, pricing or operations.

chunks.heading: Why Pavel says WhatsApp can never be secure
chunks.text:
- **Core claim:** Pavel argues that WhatsApp's security failures are structural, not accidental. His stated position is that "backdoors in WhatsApp would keep getting discovered, and one serious security issue would follow another."
- **Scope of the damage:** He says WhatsApp's flaws compromise more than WhatsApp messages. A hacker only had to send a user a video to put all data on the phone at the attacker's mercy. He calls the app "a Trojan horse" used to spy on non-WhatsApp photos and messages.

chunks.heading: Why Pavel doubts Facebook's intentions
chunks.text:
- Pavel notes that Facebook was part of surveillance programs (he cites PRISM and the NSA's data taps on major net firms) before it acquired WhatsApp.
- He calls it "naive to think the company would change its policies after the acquisition."
- He points to WhatsApp co-founder Brian Acton's admission about the sale to Facebook: "I sold my users' privacy."
- His conclusion: WhatsApp is "a honeypot for people that still trust Facebook in 2019."

chunks.heading: How Pavel reads Facebook's "no evidence of exploitation" defense
chunks.text:
- Facebook said it had no evidence the video backdoor had been exploited by hackers.
- Pavel calls this a deliberate confusion of the public. His reasoning is that Facebook can't have evidence because it can't analyze the videos users share. WhatsApp doesn't permanently store video files on its servers.
- He adds that WhatsApp sends unencrypted messages and media of "the vast majority of their users" straight to Google's and Apple's servers (the cloud backup issue). So there is "nothing to analyze," hence "no evidence. Convenient."
- He argues a flaw of this magnitude is "bound to have been exploited."

chunks.heading: The track record Pavel cites
chunks.text:
- The previous WhatsApp backdoor was used against human rights activists and journalists. Pavel cites reports of about 100 journalists and dissidents targeted, and of government officials around the globe targeted through WhatsApp.
- He cites a September 2019 report that data obtained through such backdoors will be shared with other countries by US agencies, and notes a UK deal that gives police access to suspects' Facebook and WhatsApp messages.
- Three WhatsApp backdoors are referenced in sequence: the latest (the video flaw), the previous one, and the one before that.

chunks.heading: Telegram comparison and the "accident vs. design" argument
chunks.text:
- Pavel concedes it might be coincidence that WhatsApp "accidentally implements critical security vulnerabilities across all their apps every few months," but says "I doubt that."
- His benchmark: Telegram, "a similar app in its complexity," has had no issues of WhatsApp-level severity in the six years since its 2013 launch.
- His inference: "It's very unlikely that anyone can accidentally commit major security errors, conveniently suitable for surveillance, on a regular basis."

chunks.heading: Pavel's advice to users
chunks.text: - Regardless of the underlying intentions of WhatsApp's parent company, the advice is the same: "unless you are cool with all your photos and messages becoming public one day, you should delete WhatsApp from your phone."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains how Telegram prepared for Russia's April 2018 ban by shipping rotating proxies and traffic-hiding tools, and by mobilising volunteer engineers. Despite the block, Russian users doubled, showing growth in a hostile market can match growth elsewhere when distribution does not depend on gatekeepers.

chunks.heading: Telegram survived Russia's block by shipping anti-censorship tech before the ban landed
chunks.text:
- Roskomnadzor blocked Telegram in Russia in April 2018.
- Pavel's team knew the block was coming and prepared in advance.
- By the time the block went live, the apps already supported rotating proxy servers, ways to hide traffic and other anti-censorship tools.
- The first week of the ban was still rough, and many Russian users had connection issues.
- Roskomnadzor blacklisted millions of IP addresses to stop access.
- After May 2018, Telegram was largely accessible in Russia anyway.

chunks.heading: Decentralised community support turned a ban into a growth non-event
chunks.text:
- Thousands of Russian engineers set up their own proxy servers for Telegram users.
- The result was a decentralised movement called "Digital Resistance".
- Pavel credits this movement with restoring access after the first week.
- Telegram did not have to run all of the counter-measures itself. Users and volunteers carried a large part of the load.

chunks.heading: The ban did not shrink the user base
chunks.text:
- Telegram's Russian user base has doubled since 2018.
- In May 2020, Telegram had 400 million monthly active users. At least 30 million of them were in Russia.
- Growth in Russia kept pace with growth in other countries.
- Pavel's verdict: "the ban didn't work."
- Roskomnadzor, under a director who had been in the role for two months, announced Telegram was no longer blocked. The announcement referenced Pavel's 4 June message explaining why the ban made little sense.

chunks.heading: Staying ahead of the censors requires constant upgrades
chunks.text:
- Over two years, Telegram had to regularly upgrade its "unblocking" technology to stay ahead of the censors.
- Pavel calls the result unique among social media apps and says he is proud of it.
- If the block returns, he hopes few users will notice any difference.

chunks.heading: Redeploying anti-censorship capability instead of letting it decay
chunks.text:
- Pavel does not want the technology to "get rusty and obsolete".
- Telegram is redirecting its anti-censorship resources to places where governments still ban it, such as Iran and China.
- He asks the admins of the former Russian proxy servers to focus their efforts on those countries.
- He expects more governments to try to block privacy-focused apps like Telegram as the political situation becomes more unpredictable, and wants the volunteers ready for that.
- Framing: "The Digital Resistance movement doesn't end with last week's ceasefire in Russia. It is just getting started – and going global."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov argues that Apple's 30% commission on app sales is a platform-level tax that raises prices, forces ad-based business models, kills marginal apps and erodes privacy. It's a lesson in how platform fees distort pricing, product quality and which business models survive.

chunks.heading: Why Apple's 30% commission raises costs for users and developers alike
chunks.text:
Pavel argues that Apple's 30% App Store commission is added on top of everything else developers already pay. He sees it as a tax that ends up costing iPhone users money, choice, privacy, and app quality. He lists seven reasons users should care.

- **Higher prices.** The 30% sits on top of what users pay developers for apps, services and games.
  - Users already paid "a few hundred dollars more" for the iPhone than it cost to make.
  - His summary: "you keep paying even after you have paid."

chunks.heading: Apple's control of the App Store enables censorship
chunks.text:
- Some content in apps like Telegram is unavailable on iPhone because Apple controls what the App Store allows.
- He says Apple controls the store in order to enforce the 30% tax.
- Apple also bars developers from telling users that specific content was hidden for iPhone users at their request.
- He compares it to a web browser deciding which websites you may view, and calls Apple's global censorship attempt "ridiculous".

chunks.heading: Mandatory Apple accounts weaken user privacy
chunks.text:
- Installing an app requires creating an Apple account and logging in.
- Every app downloaded and every push notification received is then tied to that account, which makes the user easier to track.
- He says the main reason an Apple account is required is Apple's wish to enforce the 30% commission, so "the cost of their greed also includes your private data."

chunks.heading: Slow app review delays updates
chunks.text:
- Users get new app versions days or weeks after they are ready because Apple's review team is "notoriously inefficient" and often delays approval for no apparent reason.
- Big apps like Telegram typically wait several days to publish updates.
- He points out that Apple receives billions of dollars from third-party apps and could hire more moderators, yet apparently cannot.

chunks.heading: The commission makes many apps unviable and leads to fewer apps
chunks.text:
- The 30% adds to other developer costs: government taxes such as VAT (about 20%), wages, research, servers and marketing.
- Many apps would be net profitable without the commission, but surrendering 30% of revenue makes them unsustainable.
- Many go bankrupt, so "lots of great apps you could have enjoyed just don't exist."

chunks.heading: Business model effects: more ads and worse apps
chunks.text:
- Selling premium services and accepting donations becomes "one-third less meaningful" for developers.
- Many therefore show ads to survive, which skews the industry toward selling user data.
- He prefers privacy-friendly models such as selling additional services to users.
- Billions taken from developers could otherwise fund app quality and R&D.
- Instead, he says the money "rests idly in Apple's offshore bank accounts and does nothing for the world."

chunks.heading: Why the 30% cut has survived for over 10 years
chunks.text:
- Pavel notes the situation is bad enough that the cut should be unsustainable, yet it has existed for more than 10 years.
- He says Apple tricked consumers and regulators into inaction.
- He pointed readers to a longer Telegraph post explaining how Apple managed this.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains how Telegram will fund growth toward billions of users without selling out. The plan keeps core features free, charges power users and businesses, runs ads only in public one-to-many channels, and shares revenue with creators.

chunks.heading: Why Telegram must monetize and stay independent
chunks.text:
- As Telegram nears 500 million active users, Pavel says a project of its size needs "at least a few hundred million dollars per year" for traffic and servers.
- He covered Telegram's expenses from personal savings for most of its history.
- He sees two options at this scale: earn money to cover costs, or sell the company.
- He rejects selling: "We are not going to sell the company like the founders of Whatsapp."
- His reasoning: Telegram must stay independent so users are respected and service quality is high, and he argues that is impossible once a company becomes part of a corporation.
- He wants Telegram to serve as an example of a tech company that strives for perfection and integrity.
- He frames Telegram as long-term: development began over 8 years earlier for personal use, and he says "This journey has just started."

chunks.heading: Monetization principles: non-intrusive, started next year
chunks.text:
- Telegram will begin generating revenue starting in 2021, in line with its values and pledges from the previous 7 years.
- He argues that current scale makes it possible to monetize in a non-intrusive way: "Most users will hardly notice any change."
- The stated goal is funding that keeps Telegram independent, innovating, and able to grow to billions of users for decades.
- He wants to redefine how a tech company should operate while staying true to its values.

chunks.heading: Free tier stays free, paid features for power users
chunks.text:
- Everything currently free stays free.
- New paid features will target business teams and power users.
- Some of these features need more resources, so premium users pay for them.
- Regular users keep Telegram "for free, forever."
- Pricing logic: charge the heavy users whose usage costs more, not the mass of regular users.

chunks.heading: Messaging stays ad-free
chunks.text:
- All messaging parts of Telegram remain ad-free.
- He considers ads in private 1-to-1 chats or group chats "a bad idea."
- His principle: "Communication between people should be free of advertising of any sort."

chunks.heading: Ad Platform for public one-to-many channels
chunks.text:
- Telegram has a social networking side besides messaging. Public one-to-many channels can have millions of subscribers each and work more like Twitter feeds.
- Channel owners in many markets already display ads, sometimes via third-party ad platforms. Those ads look like regular messages and are often intrusive.
- His fix: Telegram's own Ad Platform for public channels that is user-friendly, respects privacy, and covers server and traffic costs.
- Ads are confined to public broadcast channels, not private communication.

chunks.heading: Sharing revenue with the community
chunks.text:
- His principle: if Telegram earns money, the community should benefit too.
- Ad Platform example: owners of large public channels monetized through it receive free traffic in proportion to their size.
- Premium stickers example: if Telegram introduces premium stickers with additional expressive features, the artists who make them get a part of the profit.
- Goal: "We want millions of Telegram-based creators and small businesses to thrive, enriching the experience of all our users."
- He calls this approach "the Telegram way."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov argues Telegram's growth comes from respecting users rather than marketing. He contrasts Telegram's zero ad spend and verifiable openness with Facebook's ~$10B marketing budget and WhatsApp's forced data-sharing terms, and rebuts three myths pushed against Telegram.

chunks.heading: Respect for users as the core growth strategy
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram's "secret" is simple: "respect your users." He offers it to Facebook for free, joking that Facebook has dozens of employees working full-time on why Telegram is popular and could save "tens of millions of dollars."
- He contrasts this with WhatsApp's January 2021 Terms change, which required users to feed their private data to Facebook's ad engine. He credits that change with accelerating a user flight from WhatsApp to Telegram that had already been under way for a few years.
- At about 500 million users and growing, Telegram has become a major problem for Facebook, in Pavel's framing. His claim is that WhatsApp cannot compete with Telegram on quality and privacy.

chunks.heading: Zero marketing spend
chunks.text:
- Pavel states that Telegram "doesn't spend any money, let alone billions of dollars, on marketing."
- His comparison point: Facebook spent almost $10 billion on marketing in 2019.
- His rationale: "We believe that people are smart enough to choose what is best for them." He treats roughly half a billion users as proof that this belief is justified.
- He describes the growth model as users choosing the product on its merits (quality and privacy) rather than being persuaded by paid promotion.

chunks.heading: Competitors' covert marketing and how Telegram responds
chunks.text:
- Pavel accuses WhatsApp of switching to covert marketing because it cannot compete on quality and privacy. His evidence: Wikipedia editors exposed multiple paid bots adding biased information to the WhatsApp article. In December 2020 that article carried the label "This article may have been created or edited in return for undisclosed payments."
- He says Telegram has also detected bots spreading inaccurate information about it on social media.
- His response is public rebuttal with verifiable facts, not counter-spending. He lists the three myths and answers each with specifics (next two sections).

chunks.heading: Myth 1: "Telegram's code is not open-source"
chunks.text:
- All Telegram client apps have been open source since 2013.
- Telegram's encryption and API are fully documented and, he says, have been reviewed by security experts thousands of times.
- Telegram is the only messaging app in the world with verifiable (reproducible) builds for both iOS and Android.
- By contrast, he says WhatsApp intentionally obfuscates its code, making its encryption and privacy impossible to verify.
- His principle: back trust claims with things users and experts can check themselves.

chunks.heading: Myths 2 and 3: "Telegram is Russian" and "Telegram is not encrypted"
chunks.text:
**"Telegram is Russian"**
- Telegram has no servers or offices in Russia.
- It was blocked in Russia from 2018 to 2020.
- It is still blocked in some authoritarian countries such as Iran, while WhatsApp and other "supposedly secure" apps have never had an issue there. He uses this as evidence of independence.

**"Telegram is not encrypted"**
- Every chat on Telegram has been encrypted since launch.
- Secret Chats are end-to-end encrypted.
- Cloud Chats offer real-time secure and distributed cloud storage.
- He contrasts this with WhatsApp: zero encryption for a few years, then an encryption protocol funded by the US Government. Even if that encryption is solid, he says it is invalidated by multiple backdoors and reliance on backups.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov answers fears about Telegram ads by laying out a privacy-first monetization stance. Chats stay ad-free, ads appear only in large one-to-many channels, targeting is contextual rather than based on user data, and the goal is to replace chaotic third-party ad networks and give creators sustainable income.

chunks.heading: Ads on Telegram: no ads in chats
chunks.text:
- Pavel says Telegram will never show ads in private chats or group chats. They "are and will always be ad-free."
- Ads are considered only for large one-to-many channels, which don't exist in other messaging apps.
- Users who rely on Telegram as a messaging app, not a social network, will never see ads.
- Pavel's pitch to people switching from older apps is that switching won't increase the number of ads in their lives.
- This is how he answers an article warning users away from Telegram because "Telegram is going to introduce ads."

chunks.heading: Contextual ads, no user data targeting
chunks.text:
- Pavel calls collecting private data to target ads "the way WhatsApp-Facebook do" immoral.
- He points to privacy-conscious services like DuckDuckGo as the model: monetize the service without collecting information about users.
- Any ads in one-to-many channels would be contextual, based on the topic of the channel and not on any user data.
- Positioning point: refusing data-driven targeting is both a principle and a differentiator against WhatsApp and Facebook.

chunks.heading: Fixing the existing channel ad market
chunks.text:
- In most markets, content creators on Telegram already monetize by selling promotional posts in their channels.
- Pavel describes this as a chaotic market. Multiple third-party ad networks push intrusive ads that create a negative user experience.
- Telegram's plan is to fix this by offering channel owners a privacy-conscious alternative to those networks.
- His framing: the ads are already there, so an official, cleaner option improves the experience instead of adding to it.

chunks.heading: Opt-out and creator monetization options
chunks.text:
- Users will be able to opt out of ads.
- Pavel considers privacy-conscious ads a good way for channel owners to monetize their efforts.
- Ads are one option among several. He names donations and subscriptions as alternatives, and says Telegram is also working to offer those.
- The aim is to give channel owners a choice of monetization strategies and not a single mandatory one.

chunks.heading: Building a financially sustainable creator class
chunks.text:
- Pavel's stated end goal is a new class of content creators who are financially sustainable and free to choose the strategy that is best for their subscribers.
- He argues traditional social networks have "exploited users and publishers for far too long with excessive data collection and manipulative algorithms."
- His message: "It's time to change this."
- Strategy pattern: align creator income with subscriber trust by giving creators tools (ads, donations, subscriptions) without surveillance or algorithmic manipulation.

chunks.heading: Answering criticism of a planned monetization move
chunks.text:
- Pavel rebuts the critical article point by point with three numbered reasons: no ads in chats, no data-based targeting, and fixing ads that already exist.
- He ties the answer to a December announcement in which he had already outlined that ads were being considered only for large channels.
- The tactic is to narrow the claim precisely (which surfaces, which data, which users) so "Telegram is going to introduce ads" is shown to be misleading.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2021 essay arguing that centralization of platforms, payments and surveillance is eroding individual freedoms, while the most talented builders are absorbed by attention-harvesting products. It frames Durov's worldview behind Telegram: privacy and independence from gatekeepers. Little tactical growth or pricing advice.

chunks.heading: Individual freedoms are declining, and Big Tech controls the choke points
chunks.text:
Pavel argues that on individual freedoms, the world is getting worse rather than better, despite the common assumption of yearly progress. He says most studies show humanity is now less free than several years ago.

- His comparison point: 20 years earlier (from his 2021-08-30 post), the Internet was decentralized and banking was relatively unrestricted.
- Today, he says, "Apple and Google censor information and apps on our phones while Visa and Mastercard limit what goods and services we can pay for."
- His summary of the trend: "Every year we give up more power and control over our lives to a handful of unaccountable corporate executives we didn't elect."

chunks.heading: Platform gatekeepers: app stores and payment networks
chunks.text:
For Pavel, the control points are the layers every product depends on to reach users and get paid.

- **Distribution:** Apple and Google decide which apps and information appear on people's phones.
- **Payments:** Visa and Mastercard decide which goods and services people can pay for.
- He describes these as concentrated, unaccountable corporate power, with executives nobody elected setting the limits.
- Implication he draws: a builder's reach and revenue depend on a few intermediaries, and that dependence keeps growing.

chunks.heading: Surveillance and attention capture
chunks.text:
Pavel criticizes the personal-data business model behind much of the consumer Internet.

- Most people "willingly carry tracking devices", meaning their phones.
- Corporations use users' private data to target them with content that keeps them distracted with low-quality entertainment.
- He also notes the spread of surveillance cameras, which in countries like China use AI "to make sure nobody can hide."
- His position is that tracking and ad targeting are tools for capturing attention rather than serving users.

chunks.heading: Authoritarian growth as a competing model
chunks.text:
Pavel points to China's economic rise as a driver of the freedom decline.

- In 2017, China overtook the US as the largest economy in the world by purchasing power.
- He says this showed the world that "individual freedoms are not required for economic development."
- His claim is that, looking at China's success, more countries become authoritarian, curbing essential human rights such as freedom of speech, movement and assembly.

chunks.heading: Where talent is going, and who will fix it
chunks.text:
Pavel asks who will reverse the trend, and he is critical of the answer.

- The most active and creative minds of his generation are "too busy playing in the rapidly shrinking sandbox called 'free enterprise'", or producing digital content that keeps everyone else glued to their devices for longer.
- Everyone else, he says, is too distracted by abundant cheap digital entertainment to assess the trend critically and act.
- He frames this as a talent-allocation problem: ambitious builders are optimizing for engagement and operating inside a narrowing space, instead of defending freedoms.

chunks.heading: Legacy framing
chunks.text:
Pavel closes with a challenge to his generation about what it will be remembered for.

- Option one: "those who let free societies turn into dystopian nightmares."
- Option two: "those who defended the freedoms that previous generations fought so hard to win."
- This frames his own work, building a platform outside the gatekeepers' reach, as part of a larger duty to defend freedoms rather than only a product choice.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov announces Telegram's first ad product, built around privacy: no ads in chats, no user-data targeting, only topic-based placement in large public channels. The post shows how to monetize a free platform to cover costs while sharing revenue with creators and positioning against WhatsApp.

chunks.heading: Telegram's ad model: Sponsored Messages without user data
chunks.text:
Pavel launched Sponsored Messages in November 2021 as Telegram's first official ad product, letting anyone promote channels and bots. His central claim: "Online ads should no longer be synonymous with the abuse of user privacy."

- Telegram's stated aim is to "redefine how a tech company should operate" by being a self-sustainable platform that respects users and content creators.
- At launch the product was in test mode and not available to everyone.

chunks.heading: Targeting by channel topic, not by user data
chunks.text:
Pavel's privacy principle is that advertisers never get private data and none is mined to pick ads.

- Ads are matched solely to the topic of the public channel where they appear.
- No user data is analyzed or used for targeting.
- Pavel contrasts this with other apps: "unlike other apps we will not use your private data to display ads."
- He notes WhatsApp already shares user data with advertisers even though it shows no ads itself, while on Telegram "advertisers will never get your private data."

chunks.heading: Where ads appear: keeping the core messenger ad-free
chunks.text:
Pavel draws a hard line around the personal messaging experience.

- No ads in chats. Sponsored messages can't appear in the chat list, private chats or groups.
- They show only in large public one-to-many channels with 1000+ members.
- Anyone using Telegram "the way you use WhatsApp" will never see a single ad.
- He argues channels are a feature added several years after launch (the messenger launched in 2013), so ads sit in a separate layer from the original product.
- He predicts that if WhatsApp adds a similar feature, it will likely show ads there too, as its parent company already does on Instagram and Facebook.

chunks.heading: Unobtrusive ad format
chunks.text:
Pavel limits the format so ads stay light.

- Maximum 160 characters of text.
- No media and no external links.
- At most one sponsored message per channel.
- Shown only after the user has finished reading any new posts.

chunks.heading: Cleaning up the existing ad mess
chunks.text:
Pavel frames the product as a fix for something already happening.

- Some channel admins already post ads as regular messages.
- He hopes Sponsored Messages become a more user-friendly and less chaotic way for people to promote their channels and bots.
- In effect, a native, constrained ad product replaces ad-hoc paid posts.

chunks.heading: Monetization and revenue sharing
chunks.text:
Pavel sequences the economics: cover costs first, then share.

- Once the product is fully launched and covers Telegram's basic costs, he plans to share ad revenue with the admins of channels where the ads display.
- Costs he names: equipment and data centers used by channel admins to deliver content to "hundreds of millions" of users.
- His rationale for sharing: "because it is fair."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains how Telegram resisted Stories until user demand forced the issue, then adapted the format to Telegram's strengths: granular privacy, a compact UI, optional ephemerality and viral reposts from channels. It shows a product philosophy of listening to users while innovating on existing formats.

chunks.heading: Why Pavel resisted Stories, then built them anyway
chunks.text:
- Pavel says "more than half of all feature requests" Telegram receives are about Stories.
- He was initially against building them, since Stories are "already everywhere."
- He argues Telegram "wouldn't be Telegram" if it ignored user demand or failed to "innovate on existing formats."
- Rule he follows: let user demand override personal skepticism, but never copy a format as is. Rework it to fit the product's identity.
- Internal testing converted skeptics on his own team: "We can no longer imagine Telegram without it."

chunks.heading: Privacy as the core differentiator
chunks.text:
- Pavel makes privacy the first pillar of Telegram's version of an existing feature.
- Each story gets its own audience, with granular control:
  - Everyone
  - Only contacts (with exceptions)
  - A few selected contacts
  - A Close Friends list
- Any contact's Stories can be hidden into a "Hidden" list in the Contacts section instead of the main screen.
- Takeaway: when entering a crowded category, he differentiates on control for the user rather than on novelty for its own sake.

chunks.heading: Compact UI that protects existing screen space
chunks.text:
- Stories sit in an expandable section at the top of the chat list.
- Pavel's stated goal: make them "easily accessible without taking away valuable space."
- Design rule he applies: a new feature should not displace the core experience (the chat list).

chunks.heading: Flexible expiry and permanent profile content
chunks.text:
- Ephemerality is optional. Creators choose expiry of 6, 12, 24 or 48 hours, or display stories permanently on their profile page.
- Each option carries individual privacy settings.
- Pavel expects saved stories to make profiles "more informative and colorful."
- Business effect he points to: users can learn more about people they meet in groups or channel comments, which deepens connections beyond chat.

chunks.heading: Building on existing Telegram strengths
chunks.text:
- Dual Camera Support builds on "the success of Telegram's Video Messages." Front and rear cameras record simultaneously.
- Captions add context, links and people tagging, alongside "dozens of powerful photo and video-editing tools."
- Pattern: he extends formats Telegram already won with rather than bolting on a clone.

chunks.heading: Stories as a growth and virality lever for channels
chunks.text:
- Pavel says channels "will benefit from more exposure and subscribers" once messages can be reposted from channels to stories.
- His claim: this makes "going viral on Telegram" a lot easier.
- Distribution logic: add a sharing path from content inside the app to a high-visibility surface, so creators gain subscribers.

chunks.heading: Launch approach
chunks.text:
- Feature was in its "last testing phase," with release planned for "early July" 2023 (post dated 2023-06-26).
- He announces it in advance via his channel, teases "more surprises," and follows with a preview in the next post.
- Framing: it "will herald a new era on Telegram, where it will become even more fun and social."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After his arrest in France, Durov explains Telegram's stance on privacy versus security. He argues platforms, not CEOs, should be held accountable, says Telegram will exit markets that conflict with its principles, and commits to improving moderation after growth to 950M users.

chunks.heading: Pavel's account of the Paris arrest and why he argues it was misguided
chunks.text:
Pavel says he was interviewed by French police for 4 days after arriving in Paris. He was told he might be personally responsible for other people's illegal use of Telegram, because French authorities said they got no responses from Telegram. He disputes the premise on three grounds:

- **Reachable representative:** Telegram has an official EU representative that accepts and replies to EU requests. Its email address is publicly findable by googling "Telegram EU address for law enforcement".
- **Direct access to him:** As a French citizen, he was a frequent guest at the French consulate in Dubai. He personally helped French authorities set up a hotline with Telegram to deal with terrorism threats.
- **Wrong legal target:** The established practice, he says, is to take legal action against the service itself. Charging a CEO with crimes committed by third parties, using "laws from the pre-smartphone era", is in his words "a misguided approach".

chunks.heading: Founder liability and its effect on innovation
chunks.text:
Pavel argues that personal liability for users' abuse of a tool kills building. His reasoning:

- "Building technology is hard enough as it is."
- "No innovator will ever build new tools if they know they can be personally held responsible for potential abuse of those tools."
- Regulators should pursue the platform as a legal entity, not the executive.

chunks.heading: Balancing privacy and security as a platform
chunks.text:
Pavel describes this balance as hard and lists what a platform has to reconcile:

- Privacy laws versus law enforcement requirements.
- Local laws versus EU laws.
- Technological limitations.
- A platform wants consistent processes globally, but those processes must not be abused in countries with weak rule of law.

He says Telegram has been committed to engaging with regulators to find the right balance. Its principles are shaped by a mission to protect users in authoritarian regimes, but it has "always been open to dialogue".

chunks.heading: Willingness to exit markets rather than compromise principles
chunks.text:
When Telegram and a regulator cannot agree on the balance, Pavel says Telegram is ready to leave that country, and has done so many times:

- **Russia:** Russia demanded "encryption keys" to enable surveillance. Telegram refused and was banned in Russia.
- **Iran:** Iran demanded Telegram block channels of peaceful protesters. Telegram refused and was banned in Iran.

His stated rationale: "we are not doing this for money." Telegram is driven by the intention to bring good and defend basic rights, particularly where those rights are violated. He frames being prepared to lose markets as the cost of staying compatible with the product's principles.

chunks.heading: Moderation facts he cites against the "anarchic paradise" claim
chunks.text:
Pavel rejects media claims that Telegram is an anarchic paradise. His evidence:

- Telegram takes down millions of harmful posts and channels every day.
- It publishes daily transparency reports.
- It has direct hotlines with NGOs to process urgent moderation requests faster.

chunks.heading: Admitting gaps and committing to improve
chunks.text:
Pavel concedes Telegram is not perfect and names specific problems to fix:

- Authorities being confused about where to send requests is something Telegram "should improve".
- The abrupt jump in user count to 950M caused growing pains that made it easier for criminals to abuse the platform.
- He made it his personal goal to significantly improve moderation. The process had already started internally, with details on progress promised "very soon".

He hopes the events will make Telegram, and the social networking industry as a whole, safer and stronger.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov recounts building VKontakte alone in 2006: start with auth, build in sequence, and work obsessively. Being the only team member removed communication overhead and gave him full-stack product knowledge. VK hit a million members within months and 100M monthly users in seven years.

chunks.heading: How Pavel built VK solo as a way to stay in touch with classmates
chunks.text:
- Pavel launched VK (VKontakte, "in contact") on October 10, 2006, his first large company.
- The origin was personal: after graduating from Saint-Petersburg University in summer 2006, he wanted to keep in touch with classmates. He knew that would be hard without a site where everyone could find each other.
- In late August 2006 he set a goal of building a social network for university students and graduates in four weeks.
- It took six weeks instead of four. He calls the plan "overconfident", but says the result was worth it.

chunks.heading: Build everything from scratch, alone
chunks.text:
- Pavel decided not to use any ready-made third-party modules. He built profiles, private messages, photo albums and search himself.
- His coding background: at 12 he built web games with vector animations and sound effects, and at 13 he taught Pascal to older kids in summer camps for programmers.
- Being the only team member minimized time spent on internal communication.
- Because he knew every line of the code base by heart, he could find and fix bugs faster.
- He tried to make each section flawless. He admits that obsessing over details did not help him hit the four-week target.

chunks.heading: Split a big task into small ones and sequence them
chunks.text:
- The task initially "seemed too large to grasp". His brother Nikolai, a mathematician and algorithmic programmer then working on his thesis at the Max Planck University in Bonn, advised: "Write the code for user authorization first. You'll get through."
- Pavel started with a login page that generated session IDs. Sessions identified users, showed their profile pages and let them edit them.
- He deferred sign-up entirely. He prepopulated the database entries for the first few users manually.
- His lesson: "Every complex task is just a combination of many simple ones." If you split a big project into manageable parts and arrange them in the right order, you can get anything done.
- He adds that in practice you also hit technical obstacles that test your persistence.

chunks.heading: Extreme focus during the build
chunks.text:
- In September 2006 he typically coded 20 hours in a row, ate one meal, then slept 10 hours.
- His food was a bucket of boiled pasta with a generous amount of cheese. He says no other food was required.
- He did not care whether it was day or night, and social connections "stopped existing". All that mattered was the code.

chunks.heading: Launch, early growth and a seeded audience
chunks.text:
- The beta went live on October 10, 2006.
- Users invited from his earlier project, a students' portal he had been building since 2003, signed up by the thousands and started inviting friends.
- He kept adding new features quickly, and competitors struggled to catch up.
- A few months after launch he hired a second developer. By then VK already had a million members.
- Within seven years VK reached 100 million monthly users. At that point the VK board fired him, and he left to focus fully on Telegram.

chunks.heading: Why being a one-person product team shaped his career
chunks.text:
- As sole member of the product team he did the work of front-end developer, back-end developer, UX/UI designer, system administrator and product manager, all at once.
- He learned the basics of each of those jobs and "the tiniest details of how a social network works".
- He says this experience was so valuable that it defined his career.
- His closing principle: "there are no complex tasks in this world, only many small ones that look scary when combined". Split a big task into smaller parts, organize them in the right sequence, and "you'll get through".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov argues China's AI catch-up (DeepSeek) stems from an education system that embraces competition and public rankings, borrowed from the Soviet model. Western schools that hide grades demotivate top students and mask the public rankings reality eventually imposes.

chunks.heading: Competition and public rankings drive excellence in education
chunks.text:
- Pavel argues China's secondary education system is superior to the West's at producing outstanding performers in math and science.
- Evidence he cites: Chinese students have long outperformed others in math and programming at international olympiads.
- Pavel says China fosters fierce competition among students, a principle borrowed from the highly efficient Soviet model.
- He contrasts this with most Western schools, which discourage competition and prohibit public announcements of students' grades and rankings.
- He grants the rationale ("to protect students from pressure or ridicule") but says the measures predictably demotivate the best students.
- His core principle: "Victory and defeat are two sides of the same coin. Eliminate the losers — and you eliminate the winners."

chunks.heading: Motivation comes from visible rankings
chunks.text:
- Pavel says many students are motivated to excel by treating high school as a competitive game, striving to rank first against strong opponents.
- Removing transparency in student performance can make school feel meaningless for ambitious teenagers.
- He observes that many gifted kids now find competitive gaming more exciting than academics, because in video games they can see how each player ranks.
- Takeaway for product and community design: visible leaderboards and rankings are a motivator for ambitious people, and removing them demotivates the strongest performers.

chunks.heading: Reality has public grades and rankings
chunks.text:
- Pavel argues that telling all students they are champions regardless of performance may seem kind, but reality will shatter the illusion quickly after graduation.
- In his words, reality "does have public grades and rankings — whether in sports, business, science, or technology."
- He treats public benchmarks as the real-world equivalent of school grades, and says "more are coming."
- Example he gives: the AI benchmarks that demonstrate DeepSeek's superiority are a public ranking.
- Implication for builders: markets and benchmarks rank products and companies openly, so teams should expect to be measured against strong competitors rather than shielded from comparison.

chunks.heading: Why China caught up in AI, and the outlook
chunks.text:
- Context: following the success of the Chinese startup DeepSeek (post dated 2025-01-29), many were surprised at how quickly China caught up with the US in AI.
- Pavel's view is that China's progress in algorithmic efficiency "hasn't come out of nothing"; it is rooted in a long-standing talent pipeline built through competitive math and programming education.
- His prediction: unless the US secondary education system undergoes radical reform, China's growing dominance in technology seems inevitable.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov argues that encryption backdoors cannot be limited to police, so they expose every law-abiding user to hackers and foreign agents, while criminals simply switch to smaller apps. He restates Telegram's stance: exit a market rather than weaken encryption, and never trade privacy for market share.

chunks.heading: Why Pavel opposes encryption backdoors
chunks.text:
- Pavel argues a backdoor can't be limited to police: "it's technically impossible to guarantee that only the police can access a backdoor."
- Once introduced, a backdoor can be exploited by other parties, "from foreign agents to hackers," so the private messages of all law-abiding citizens can be compromised.
- He frames it as a rights issue: France would have been the first country in the world to strip citizens of their right to privacy. Even countries many Europeans see as lacking in freedoms have never banned encryption.

chunks.heading: Backdoors don't stop crime
chunks.text:
- Pavel notes the French law was aimed at preventing drug trafficking, and says it wouldn't have helped fight crime anyway.
- Even if mainstream encrypted apps were weakened, criminals could still communicate securely through dozens of smaller apps.
- They would also become harder to trace because of VPNs.
- His takeaway: the policy burdens ordinary users while failing against its intended targets.

chunks.heading: Telegram's policy: exit a market rather than weaken encryption
chunks.text:
- Pavel states that "Telegram would rather exit a market than undermine encryption with backdoors and violate basic human rights."
- He positions this against competitors: "Unlike some of our competitors, we don't trade privacy for market share."
- Privacy is treated as a non-negotiable principle that outranks growth in any single country.

chunks.heading: What Telegram will and won't disclose to authorities
chunks.text:
- In its 12-year history (as of April 2025), Telegram "has never disclosed a single byte of private messages."
- Under the EU Digital Services Act, with a valid court order, Telegram would disclose only the IP addresses and phone numbers of criminal suspects, not messages.
- This sets a clear line: cooperate narrowly and lawfully on identifiers, never on message content.

chunks.heading: The 2025 French and EU timeline
chunks.text:
- Last month (March 2025), the French Senate passed a law requiring messaging apps to implement a backdoor for police access to private messages.
- The National Assembly shot it down.
- Three days before the post (about April 18, 2025), the Paris Police Prefect advocated for it again.
- In April 2025, the European Commission proposed a similar initiative to add backdoors to messaging apps.

chunks.heading: How Pavel says to respond: keep explaining and defending
chunks.text:
- Pavel's view is that lawmakers must keep hearing the argument that "encryption isn't built to protect criminals — it protects the privacy and safety of ordinary people."
- He treats these fights as recurring, not one-off: "The battle is far from over."
- He warns that "no country is immune to the slow erosion of freedoms" and that freedoms must be defended every day.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov explains how a "takedown extortionist" planted AI-modified illegal content by editing an old group message, then reported it to Apple, which briefly removed Telegram. He draws two lessons: app store platform risk is systemic for any user-generated-content app, and coordinated reporting attacks keep evolving.

chunks.heading: Apple removed Telegram from the App Store over planted content
chunks.text:
- On 2026-08-04, Apple briefly removed Telegram from the App Store because a single user had planted illegal pornographic content in a public group chat.
- Telegram was restored within hours.
- Pavel wrote the post to "warn other app developers and help protect online communities from similar attacks."

chunks.heading: How the attacker hid the content from moderation
chunks.text:
- Telegram removes illegal content from public groups quickly, using "all kinds of moderation tools."
- To get around this, the attacker edited an old message in an active group chat and inserted AI-modified illegal content.
- Because the edit was backdated, the content was effectively hidden from the group's members. They could not see it, so they could not report it promptly.
- Pavel treats the need for such tricks as evidence the system works: "The fact that attackers must resort to backdated, effectively invisible content and other technical tricks proves this."
- His view: illegal pornographic content in Telegram's public groups is not a systemic problem, and Telegram's moderation is effective.

chunks.heading: Takedown extortion: the attacker's business model
chunks.text:
- The attacker was a "takedown extortionist": someone who demands ransom from group owners in exchange for not targeting their communities.
- The method:
  - Automated accounts plant illegal content in public groups.
  - The extortionists report it directly to Apple.
  - The aim is to trigger the removal of legitimate communities whose owners refused to pay.
- Pavel notes the tactics are evolving, which puts communities across social platforms at risk.

chunks.heading: Platform risk: Apple removed the app before contacting Telegram
chunks.text:
- Extortionists have found a way to manipulate Apple into overreacting.
- Apple removed Telegram before contacting the company.
- Pavel's argument: "If an app used by more than a billion people can be removed from the App Store without prior warning, any app can be."
- He calls this a potential systemic risk for every mobile app that hosts user-generated content.
- Takeaway for developers: dependence on a single app store is a distribution risk, since a single coordinated report can cut off even a billion-user app.

chunks.heading: Defending communities against coordinated reporting
chunks.text:
- Telegram has extensive experience identifying the tricks used by coordinated reporting gangs and protecting legitimate communities.
- Pavel says Telegram does this even when it risks its own app being temporarily removed from the App Store, showing he prioritizes protecting communities over avoiding store-level risk.
- He warns that other platforms may not be equally prepared.
- His closing advice to developers and community owners: "Stay vigilant!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Two years after his detention in Paris, Durov argues Telegram's moderation and cooperation with authorities are no worse than other major platforms. He describes a pattern where platforms refusing secret political demands get hit with orchestrated media and NGO campaigns. Mostly a political essay with limited growth or business content.

chunks.heading: What the French case reveals: selective enforcement against Telegram
chunks.text:
Two years after his Paris detention (held 3 days, the longest police can hold someone before charging), Pavel argues the French case is losing credibility. He calls it unprecedented: "French authorities accused the head of a major platform of crimes committed by its users." He says the investigation is still ongoing and "makes less sense with each passing year."

His core argument is evidence-based. Over two years, he says, extensive evidence shows Telegram was neither worse than other popular platforms at moderation nor the worst at cooperating with authorities. So the question becomes why Telegram was singled out.

chunks.heading: The pressure-then-smear pattern across countries
chunks.text:
Pavel describes a pattern he has seen in multiple countries, mostly authoritarian ones:

- Telegram is quietly pressured to grant political favors, such as illegal censorship or surveillance.
- When Telegram refuses, local media and "non-governmental" organizations launch orchestrated campaigns.
- These campaigns portray Telegram as "a cesspool of crime, from child pornography to terrorism."
- The goal is to instill the idea that Telegram should be persecuted or restricted.

He maintains that Telegram's moderation is no worse than other major platforms'.

chunks.heading: Selective concern about crime and child protection
chunks.text: Pavel argues that officials suddenly care about crime and protecting children, but only on platforms that reject their secret political demands. Platforms that accept such deals "get away with almost anything," and he claims this includes "literally selling ads promoting child pornography." The implication is that moderation enforcement is used as political leverage rather than applied evenly.

chunks.heading: Is the French investigation political?
chunks.text: Pavel says the French case "certainly fits the pattern we see elsewhere" and "definitely raises questions." He predicts that "this investigation may itself be investigated," especially now that Macron's "war against free speech" is facing pushback.

chunks.heading: Resistance to free-speech restrictions as a signal
chunks.text: As evidence of that pushback, he cites that this month (August 2026) France's Constitutional Council struck down Macron's social media ban for children under 15, on freedom-of-expression grounds. He closes with the stance that "freedom and truth will prevail."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov's Telegram posts (2017-2025) on the personal discipline behind building: avoiding alcohol and addictive substances, curating the information you consume, valuing sleep and solitude, and thinking independently instead of copying the crowd. It is about founder productivity and mindset rather than growth or pricing tactics.

chunks.heading: Health: seven things Pavel never does
chunks.text:
- Pavel avoids seven things because he found they reduce productivity and clarity of thought:
  - alcohol
  - meat (fish is fine)
  - pills and meds (except at a dentist)
  - nicotine and other addictive drugs
  - coffee, black and green tea, and energy drinks (he drinks herbal teas)
  - fast food, sugar and carbonated soft drinks
  - TV and its alternatives
- He has lived without these for many years and says he has "been feeling great and healthy".
- He does not tell people with permanent health issues to stop their medication.
- He frames the list as a tradeoff. Young, healthy people may prefer fun to productivity and can ignore it. People who "enjoy building stuff more than consuming it" may benefit from abstaining.
- In 2025 he restated it: "My success and health are the result of 20+ years of complete abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, coffee, pills, and illegal drugs. Short-term pleasure isn't worth your future."

chunks.heading: Alcohol: the one piece of advice for people in their 20s
chunks.text:
- Asked for one piece of advice for people in their 20s who want to build something great, Pavel says: "Never drink alcohol."
- He has not drunk alcohol in nearly 20 years. He has seen many successful people ruin themselves with it.
- Alcohol clouds mental clarity and intuition for days after drinking.
- He compares it to a loan: it lifts mood now, but "you'll pay it back with interest".
- He acknowledges social pressure, since humans evolved to copy those around them. He notes that most people drink alcohol, eat fast food and live passively, and says that is fine for them.
- His claim is that anyone aiming at something extraordinary improves their odds by keeping mind and body healthy.

chunks.heading: Information diet: feed the brain real-life data
chunks.text:
- Pavel says the mind is our most powerful tool and generates new ideas even when we rest. Solutions to hard problems often arrive after a full night's sleep.
- Mental state depends on the quality of information consumed, just as physical state depends on food.
- Feed the brain real-life data that lets it solve fundamental problems, and it will process that data in the background and produce unexpected solutions.
- Most people instead consume random Netflix series or TikTok videos. He says the brain cannot tell fiction from reality at a deep level, so the subconscious ends up solving problems that do not exist.
- To be creative and productive, clear the "sticky mud of irrelevant content" that recommendation algorithms push daily.
- Personal practice:
  - He never watches horror movies and prefers uplifting success stories ("Wonka" was his favorite of 2023).
  - He believes songs replayed many times work like spells that plant suggestions, so he picks lyrics without undesirable scenarios.
  - He starts the day with joyful mid-20th-century songs such as "Oh, What a Beautiful Morning" and "What a Wonderful World".
- He ties this to Telegram's design. Users get only news from channels they joined and can unsubscribe at any time, which keeps Telegram independent and lets people choose their own feed.

chunks.heading: Undervalued and overvalued things (age 37 list)
chunks.text:
- Undervalued:
  - **Sleep:** boosts immunity, creativity and psychological well-being.
  - **Nature:** the environment humans are biologically designed to feel good in.
  - **Solitude:** gives freedom for spiritual and intellectual breakthroughs.
- Overvalued:
  - **Big cities:** pollution, crime and noise. Use their resources but live outside their borders.
  - **Restaurants:** the slowest and least efficient way to eat. Home cooking gives healthier diets and ingredient control.
  - **Hot weather:** brings a lax attitude, cancer risk and faster aging. Cold "clarifies spirit, body and mind".
  - **Fashion:** conforming to trends is expensive and unnecessary. Comfortable clothes simplify life and free space for what matters.
  - **Real estate:** limits choices and is a questionable investment. Renting gives freedom to move.
  - **Social media:** the junk flow lowers happiness and creativity. Disconnecting is the best thing to do on any given day.
  - **Celebrity advice:** famous people advise outside their fields. For important things, rely on hard science and expert opinion.

chunks.heading: Independent thinking over imitation
chunks.text:
- Pavel says humans are hardwired by evolution to copy others, and for millions of years that was the most efficient survival strategy.
- In an age of rapid change, he says, copying becomes "a recipe for mediocrity and decay".
- His New Year 2025 message: rely on your own opinions, not "imposed stereotypes and outdated thought patterns".
- He argues that trusting your instincts and following your own path is how people fulfil their potential and contribute to the world.
- This links to his warning that the habits of the majority (drinking, fast food, passive lifestyles) are self-destructive.

chunks.heading: Lessons from his father (age 80)
chunks.text:
- Pavel's father is a leading expert in Ancient Roman literature. When he turned 80, Pavel asked what advice to pass to the next generation. He gave three points:
  1. **Lead by example.** People, especially kids, follow what you do, not what you say. Watching his father work tirelessly on books and scientific papers showed Pavel and his brother dedication and inspired them to work hard.
  2. **Focus on the positive.** Growing up in post-war Leningrad, his father learned to control emotions to be a positive force for family, colleagues and society. He taught Pavel to frame thoughts in ways that bring the most good, even in hard times.
  3. **Prioritize conscience.** After studying and translating thinkers from Julius Caesar to Seneca, his father concluded that morals outlast talent. Pavel calls moral compass "the ultimate human quality that will not lose value even in the age of AI".

chunks.heading: Why he defends a free Internet (age 41)
chunks.text:
- On his 41st birthday in 2025 he said he did not feel like celebrating because "our generation is running out of time to save the free Internet".
- He argues the promise of free information exchange is being turned into a tool of control, citing:
  - digital IDs (UK)
  - online age checks (Australia)
  - mass scanning of private messages (EU)
  - prosecution of online criticism in Germany, the UK and France
- He warns that his generation risks being "the last one that had freedoms — and allowed them to be taken away".
- He says people were told the main fight is to destroy tradition, privacy, sovereignty, the free market and free speech, and that this path leads to moral, intellectual, economic and biological self-destruction.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pavel Durov's channel posts trace Telegram's path from zero revenue to profit. He explains privacy-conscious ads, the Premium subscription, a stack of new monetization products and debt financing through bonds. The through-line: revenue exists to fund independence and put users first.

chunks.heading: Telegram's monetization goal: financial sustainability without losing independence
chunks.text:
- When Telegram launched, Pavel set the end goal as a financially sustainable project that "can serve humanity for decades (or centuries) to come."
- He frames monetization as a means to independence. Revenue pays for servers, traffic and wages, which keeps Telegram building features without outside control.
- His principle: "While some other apps consider their users a tool to maximize revenue, we consider revenue a tool to maximize value for our users."
- At the end of 2024 he restated it: the purpose of monetization is to ensure users "will always remain our #1 priority."
- He argues the 2024 results show that social platforms can be financially sustainable while staying independent and respecting users' rights.

chunks.heading: Privacy-conscious advertising
chunks.text:
- Telegram started monetizing in late 2021 and reviewed the first year in December 2022.
- Ad rules he set:
  - No personal data is used for targeting.
  - Promoted messages are shown only in public one-to-many channels.
- Despite these limits, he says Telegram's ads "significantly outperformed the market" and put the company on a steady path to financial sustainability.
- Ad revenue increased "a few times" in 2024.
- In 2024 he announced that ads would be sold exclusively for TON. Anticipating the concern that Telegram would hold too much Toncoin, he set a cap:
  - Telegram's share of TON is to stay at about 10% of supply.
  - The surplus goes to long-term investors under a 1-4 year lockup and vesting plan, at a discount to market price.
  - His stated aim is to lock up free-floating TON, stabilizing the ecosystem and reducing volatility.

chunks.heading: Telegram Premium: subscription growth
chunks.text:
- Premium launched around mid-2022. By December 2022, five months in, it had passed 1 million subscribers.
- He called it one of the most successful social media subscription plans ever launched. At that point it was still a fraction of revenue, but he said it "may even rival our ads" one day.
- Milestones:
  - September 2024: 10 million paid subscribers.
  - December 2024: over 12 million, with the subscriber count having tripled during 2024.

chunks.heading: Expanding the monetization stack (2024)
chunks.text:
Pavel listed the 2024 monetization innovations as:
- Stars
- Gifts
- Giveaways
- Mini Apps
- The Affiliate Platform
- Telegram Business
- Telegram Gateway

- In September 2024 he replaced People Nearby with "Businesses Nearby":
  - People Nearby was used by under 0.1% of users and had problems with bots and scammers.
  - Businesses Nearby shows legitimate, verified businesses that can display product catalogs and accept payments.
- He removes features that attract abuse and are barely used, and swaps in monetizable business features.
- He argues that the roughly 0.001% of users involved in crime damage the platform's image and put the interests of nearly a billion users at risk. He committed to turning moderation "from an area of criticism into one of praise."

chunks.heading: Profitability milestone (2024)
chunks.text:
- 2024 was the first profitable year in Telegram's 3-year history of monetization.
- Figures he gave:
  - Total revenue surpassed $1 billion.
  - Year-end cash reserves exceeded $500 million, not counting crypto assets.
  - Premium subscribers exceeded 12 million.
- By March 2025 he described Telegram as having over 1 billion monthly active users and "substantial profit."
- The Telegram bonds issued in 2021 were sold when Telegram had zero revenue and half today's user base.

chunks.heading: Funding growth with bonds instead of equity
chunks.text:
- March 2021: Telegram raised over $1 billion by selling bonds (debt) to large, knowledgeable global investors. He said this lets Telegram keep growing "while sticking to its values and remaining independent."
- Over the four years to end-2024, Telegram issued about $2 billion in debt.
- March 2024: a $330M bond issue.
  - It was oversubscribed.
  - Adjusted for the Federal Reserve rate, the terms were the most favorable in company history.
  - He read rising demand as global institutions valuing Telegram's audience and monetization growth, and as reinforcing its position to challenge the "Goliaths" of the industry.
- Autumn 2024: Telegram repaid a meaningful share of its debt, taking advantage of favorable bond prices.
- March 2025: the bonds traded at all-time highs, adjusted for the federal funds rate.
- May 2025: Telegram issued $1.7B of 5-year bonds at 9% interest, maturing June 2030.
  - More than $950M of the earlier bonds (due March 2026) were exchanged into the new issue.
  - The offering was expanded beyond the initial $1.5B because of strong demand, and demand still far exceeded what Telegram could allocate.
  - He said the proceeds leave "more than enough resources" to repay the remaining 2026 bonds.
- He credits the bondholders' support, which helps Telegram stay independent "in any economic environment."

chunks.heading: Ownership and control
chunks.text:
- Pavel states bondholders are not shareholders and have no say in Telegram's decisions. He is the sole shareholder.
- Debt rather than equity is how he funds growth without giving up control.
- In January 2026 he rebutted claims of dependence on Russian capital. The $1.7B bond offering included "exactly zero Russian investors," and the 2021 bonds had been largely repaid.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A collection of Durov's Telegram channel posts (2018-2026) on how Telegram hires through public coding contests, ships fast with a small team, rewrites core products, and argues new apps can win by copying only what works. Also covers solo-built mini apps, data portability and the cost of platform gatekeepers.

chunks.heading: Telegram's contest model: hiring and building through competitions
chunks.text:
Pavel treats crowdsourced contests as the main way Telegram finds engineers and gets work done. In 2019 he announced the Instant View 2.0 Competition, a crowdsourcing contest with a $300,000 prize fund ending on 4 April.

- The task was to write rule sets ("templates") that generate Instant View previews for links shared on Telegram. Anyone who understands HTML/CSS could take part.
- Pay was $100 for each correct template, plus $10,000 and $5,000 for the top 2 contributors.
