chunks.heading: Scale of contest spending and backing the competitive-programming world
chunks.text:
In 2026 Pavel put contests at the center of how Telegram spends on talent.

- In one month (reported 6 September 2026) Telegram awarded over $2,222,000 to winners.
- In the latest week alone $222,000 was split between the winners of the Design Contest and the Digital Freedom Contest.
- Over the same month Telegram awarded prizes worth more than $2 million to winners of the 2026 International Olympiads in Informatics and AI.
- On 11 September 2026 Telegram became the sponsor of Codeforces, the largest competitive programming platform in the world. Codeforces runs over 100 coding contests a year and has 4 million contestants signed up.
- Pavel has supported Codeforces since 2010 through the companies he started. He said this year would be special because its founder Mike wants to take Codeforces to the next level.

chunks.heading: Betting on new technology: the Swift rewrite of Telegram for iOS
chunks.text:
Pavel describes a deliberate habit of adopting new technology early.

- For a couple of years Telegram quietly rebuilt its iOS app from scratch in Swift, Apple's faster alternative to Objective C.
- The Swift version looked identical to the old one but was faster, slicker and more battery-friendly. The old app was already considered the fastest among messaging apps.
- It shipped publicly from January as a separate app called "Telegram X". Thousands of users tested it and sent feedback, which polished it before the switch.
- In September 2018 he planned to replace the default iOS app with the Swift version within a week or two. He accepted that a new codebase could bring minor bugs and promised quick fixes ("swiftly").
- This would make Telegram the most popular messaging app written fully in Swift. His view: "somebody has to take such risks and be the first to implement new technologies, such as e2e encryption – or Swift."

chunks.heading: Shipping fast and building features users ask for
chunks.text:
Pavel shows how quickly the team turns an idea into a shipped feature.

- Users wanted to move chat history from WhatsApp to Telegram. He realized two weeks before 29 January 2021 that it was theoretically possible, and the feature shipped on iOS and Android the day before his post.
- It also supports KakaoTalk and Line. He noted nothing like it had been done by a major app and the team "had to implement some serious magic" to make it work.
- Imported messages are appended to the end of the target chat but keep their original timestamps.
- Next, the team started work on merging imports into one unified timeline for target chats with fewer than 100 messages.
- He promised free APIs so third-party developers can build import tools from any app.
- Rationale: moving messages saves disk space and removes worry about third-party backups or changing devices.
- He frames this as principle: the paper plane in the Telegram logo means "freedom", and data portability and freedom of choice are paramount. "People should be in complete control over their own data – and their own lives."

chunks.heading: Copy only what works, then innovate: how Telegram and MemHash won
chunks.text:
Pavel's rule for entering a crowded market is to borrow selectively and differentiate elsewhere.

- Using the mini app MemHash as the example, he said it was built single-handedly over a weekend. It inspired dozens of copycats and created a new genre of mining mini apps on Telegram.
- His lesson: "there's always room for a new app on Telegram", provided you deeply understand which features made predecessors popular. The key is to borrow only what works while innovating and differentiating elsewhere.
- He applies the same logic to Telegram. It did not invent messaging; in 2013 it took only what was necessary from existing apps.
- It then kept listening to users and innovating, adding hundreds of useful features over 12 years. That brought popularity and helped establish a new genre of messaging.

chunks.heading: Solo builders and the mini app platform
chunks.text:
Pavel celebrates small-team and solo success on the Telegram mini app platform.

- In November 2024 he described a developer who launched a mini app that earned $500,000 in revenue within ten days of launch. It was built in two days in time off from his main job.
- With no team or marketing budget, he handled design, concept, client-side code and server-side code himself. He was inspired by Pavel's own solo journey creating VK in 2006.
- Credited drivers were a brilliant concept and minimalist design, which made it go viral. It ranked in the Top 4 grossing mini apps on Telegram for those ten days.
- Pavel's takeaway: "This is the power of hard work, determination, and the Telegram mini app platform!"

chunks.heading: Pavel's stance on app store gatekeepers
chunks.text:
Pavel argues that platform review processes slow shipping and hurt developers.

- In August 2022 he said the team is often unable to distribute new versions because of the "obscure 'review process'" imposed on mobile apps by tech monopolies.
- Telegram's update that was about to "revolutionize how people express themselves in messaging" had been stuck in Apple's review for two weeks, with no explanation or feedback.
- He noted that if a top-10 global app gets this treatment, smaller developers fare worse. The delays are demoralizing and cause direct financial losses to hundreds of thousands of apps.
- He added that this harm comes on top of the 30% tax Apple and Google take, which they say pays for app review. He said regulators in the EU and elsewhere were slowly looking into these practices, but damage already done would not be undone.
- He still voiced enthusiasm for the work itself: "What could be more exciting than improving the way hundreds of millions of people communicate?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pavel Durov's channel posts (2021-2026) track Telegram's growth from 500M to over 1B monthly users purely via word of mouth. He credits consistency in defending privacy and improving the product, algorithm-free channel distribution, and independence from advertisers and shareholders.

chunks.heading: Telegram's growth: zero marketing, word of mouth, and consistency
chunks.text:
- Pavel credits Telegram's growth to word of mouth alone: "In just a decade, Telegram gained over 800 million active users purely thanks to word of mouth" (August 2023, on Telegram's 10th birthday).
- His stated "secret" is consistency (Feb 2021): "For the last 7.5 years we've consistently defended the privacy of our users and regularly improved the quality and feature set of our apps."
- He frames this as a general rule: "Anyone who stays true to their values and applies focused effort over a long period of time is bound to succeed in their area." He says this holds for sport, blogging, art, coding, business or studying.
- Growth was steady compounding: since the 2013 launch, the user base grew over 40% each year, and Telegram became the most downloaded mobile app in the world in January 2021.
- The assumption behind the product (April 2024): "people are inherently smart. And smart people will always choose the freedom and quality of Telegram over the restrictions and mediocrity of legacy apps."

chunks.heading: User milestones, 2021-2025
chunks.text:
- Early January 2021: over 500 million monthly active users. 25 million new users joined in 72 hours. Their origin: 38% Asia, 27% Europe, 21% Latin America, 8% MENA.
- For comparison, Pavel notes that in the prior year about 1.5M new users signed up per day.
- 5 October 2021: a record day, with over 70 million "refugees from other platforms" in one day. The daily growth rate exceeded the norm by an order of magnitude.
- To retain surge users, he asked existing users to "say hi to their newly arrived friends, help them unpack, and let them know what we have in stock", and to make sure newcomers "stick around."
- July 2023: over 2.5 million new sign-ups every day and 800 million monthly active users earlier that year.
- April 2024: 900 million monthly users, with half opening Telegram daily.
- March 2025: "significantly over 1 billion" monthly active users, the second most popular messaging app in the world excluding WeChat. Each user opens Telegram 21 times a day and spends 41 minutes daily on the app.

chunks.heading: Growth driven by privacy and distrust of rivals
chunks.text:
- Pavel attributes the January 2021 surge to users refusing to trade privacy for free services: "People no longer want to exchange their privacy for free services. They no longer want to be held hostage by tech monopolies that seem to think they can get away with anything as long as their apps have a critical mass of users."
- Telegram positioned itself as "the largest refuge for those seeking a communication platform committed to privacy and security," and he calls the surge possibly "the largest digital migration in human history."
- Independence is part of the pitch: "Unlike other popular apps, Telegram doesn't have shareholders or advertisers to report to. We don't do deals with marketers, data miners or government agencies." He cites a 2018 post saying Telegram had not disclosed "a single byte" of private user data to third parties since August 2013.
- He treats Telegram as an idea more than an app: "the idea that everyone on this planet has a right to be free."
- For newcomers during migrations, the message is that Telegram is "the largest independent messaging platform. We won't fail you when others will."
- On the competition (March 2025), he calls WhatsApp "a cheap, watered-down imitation of Telegram" and says it has copied Telegram's innovations while "burning billions on lobbying and PR campaigns to slow us down. They failed."

chunks.heading: Channels as a distribution lever
chunks.text:
- Pavel argues Telegram channels are "the only direct way for opinion leaders to reliably connect with their audiences."
- Reason: "Unlike other networks, Telegram doesn't use nontransparent algorithms to decide whether a subscriber will see content they subscribed to or not." Removing manipulative algorithms "restore[s] transparency and integrity to public 'one-to-many' communication."
- Heads of state and public organizations joined the platform, which he presents as a trust signal. In January 2021 he listed the presidents of Brazil, Turkey, Mexico, France, Ukraine, Uzbekistan and Taiwan, plus the prime ministers of Singapore, Ethiopia and Israel.
- He says leaders and organizations rely on Telegram to counter misinformation and raise awareness. Verified accounts show a blue check mark in chat lists and search results.

chunks.heading: Funding growth and monetization
chunks.text:
- Scaling costs money: July 2023 growth meant "higher expenses on storage and traffic." He says Telegram is "super efficient when it comes to expenses."
- Monetization started in 2022. In July 2023 he said Telegram was not yet profitable, which he called impossible after only the second year of monetization, but was closer to profitability in absolute numbers than Twitter and Snap.
- In July 2023, Telegram issued about $270 million of bonds as a tap of existing bonds, with well-known funds participating.
- Pavel personally bought about a quarter, "tens of millions", on top of "the hundreds of millions I spent over the last 10 years to keep Telegram operational."
- He rejects personal consumption: some suggested he buy a house or a jet, but he prefers to stay focused on work, owning only Telegram, some Bitcoin and some Toncoin.
- Profitability milestones: cash flow positive in Q1 2024, on track for a profitable 2024, and $547M in profit in 2024 (as stated in March 2025). He says this "solidifies our position as an independent company that puts its users first."

chunks.heading: Next phase and growth under bans
chunks.text:
- August 2023: the next step is to "go beyond messaging and spearhead innovation in social media in general." The gradual roll-out of stories to all users marked the start of that stage.
- His stated goal is to use Telegram's popularity "to change the lives of billions for better."
- April 2026 on bans: although Telegram is banned in Russia, he says 65M Russians still use it daily via VPNs, with 50M+ sending messages every day.
- Iran banned Telegram years ago with a similar result: the government hoped for mass adoption of its own surveillance messaging apps but got mass adoption of VPNs. He cites 50M members of the "Digital Resistance" in Iran.
- His response is to keep adapting by "making Telegram's traffic harder to detect and block."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Durov's channel posts attack WhatsApp and Signal encryption claims and position Telegram as the verifiably private option. It shows competitive positioning through trust rather than paid marketing, and a product philosophy of splitting usability from security into two chat types. Claims about competitors are Durov's own assertions.

chunks.heading: Growth without marketing, and why claims must match product
chunks.text:
- In 2021 Pavel said US-based competitors were frustrated that they could not match Telegram's growth, "despite heavily investing in marketing (something Telegram has never had to invest in)".
- His argument: to match Telegram's growth, rivals "have to first make sure their actions match their marketing claims". Until then, he says, data breaches and security issues in their apps are unavoidable.
- In 2022 he cited 700M+ active users and 2M+ daily signups as the reason Telegram "doesn't need additional promotion". He said he was not pushing people to switch and that people can use any messaging app, except WhatsApp.
- Telegram's marketing posture here is to publish verifiable facts and let comparisons do the work, rather than to run campaigns.

chunks.heading: Why he says US-based messengers cannot guarantee privacy
chunks.text:
- He argues most competitors could not guarantee privacy "even if they wanted to". Their engineers live in the US and must secretly implement backdoors when the government orders it.
- An engineer who talks publicly about it can go to jail for breaching a gag order.
- He claims agencies often don't need a court order to extract data from apps like WhatsApp, and that court documents are often secret.
- He says some "secure" apps were funded by government agencies from the start, naming Anom and Signal.
- He says the NSA has long shaped international encryption standards to match what it can decipher. Other approaches get labelled "non-standard" or "home-brew", and outsiders are warned against "rolling out their own encryption".
- His conclusion is that apps built on those standards are "plagued with backdoors".

chunks.heading: Verifiability instead of "we're open source"
chunks.text:
- He calls "we are open source so anyone can verify" a trick when users cannot confirm the published code is what runs on their phones.
- He says Signal refused to add reproducible builds for iOS and closed a community GitHub request for them.
- He says WhatsApp doesn't publish its app code at all, so its privacy talk is "an even more obvious circus trick".
- His positioning of Telegram:
  - It is the only massively popular messaging service where everyone can check that its apps use the same open source code published on GitHub.
  - For ten years, Secret Chats have been "the only popular method of communication that is verifiably private".
- The principle is to make the claim checkable by outsiders rather than asking for trust.

chunks.heading: Two chat types instead of one compromise
chunks.text:
- Telegram has two types of chats: Cloud (100% usable) and Secret (100% secure).
- His claim is that apps trying to deliver both security and usability in one chat type "end up with ugly compromises".
- His two examples:
  - WhatsApp leaks about 95% of messages via unencrypted backups.
  - Signal exposes messages through push notifications. He says the FBI got deleted Signal messages just by checking notification data.
- Secret Chats never show message content in push notifications. This is enforced by design, because turning off previews doesn't help when you can't know whether the people you message have done the same.
- He admits this hurts usability, and says that is why the two-chat split exists.
- Telegram "started the end-to-end encryption revolution" 12+ years ago by launching Secret Chats. He says dozens of apps followed with bold claims, but none has beaten Cloud Chats on usability or Secret Chats on security.
- His summary of rivals: "Their try to mix the two and get neither."

chunks.heading: The WhatsApp backup argument
chunks.text:
- His April 2026 claim is that WhatsApp's "End-to-end encryption by default" is "a giant consumer fraud".
- About 95% of private WhatsApp messages end up in plain-text backups on Apple/Google servers, because backup encryption is optional and few people enable it, let alone with strong passwords.
- Even if you encrypt your own backups, your messages still land in unencrypted cloud backups, because 90%+ of the people you message haven't done the same.
- He adds that WhatsApp stores and discloses who you chat with.
- He says Apple and Google disclose backed-up WhatsApp messages to third parties thousands of times per year, while "Telegram hasn't disclosed a single byte of users' messages in its entire 12+ year history".
- In May 2026 he cited Texas suing WhatsApp for lying about privacy, because employees allegedly have access to "virtually all" private messages. He tied this to the WhatsApp founder's remark that he "sold his users' privacy".

chunks.heading: Security track record as a positioning argument
chunks.text:
- In 2022 he argued that WhatsApp has had a serious security flaw disclosed almost every year (2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, and again in 2022, when a malicious video or video call could give full phone access). He says these are not accidents but planted backdoors that get replaced when removed.
- He noted that WhatsApp had no encryption at all before 2016, and called it a surveillance tool for 13 years.
- He used Jeff Bezos's 2020 phone compromise as evidence that even the richest person's data was exposed.
- He said he deleted WhatsApp from his own devices years ago, because "having it installed creates a door to get into your phone".
- A pattern in his tactics: he cites a news hook (a report, a lawsuit, an FBI case, a disclosed vulnerability) and links it to a structural claim about the competitor.

chunks.heading: Signal's origins as a trust argument
chunks.text:
- In 2024 he amplified a story from Twitter founder Jack Dorsey, claiming Signal's current leaders are activists used by the US State Department for regime change abroad.
- He claimed the US government spent $3M to build Signal's encryption, and that the same encryption now runs in WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, Google Messages and Skype.
- His reading: big US tech "is not allowed to build its own encryption protocols that would be independent of government interference".
- He said many important people told him their "private" Signal messages had been used against them in US courts or media.
